title: Show HN: My AI induced mania in embedded computer graphics engineering [video]
author: i2pi
body:
Author: superchromat

20 years ago on the venerable DailyWTF programming blog, the inner-platform effect anti-pattern was named and shamed. Now, this pattern is an invariable sort of consequence of the collective insanity of enterprise software engineering where the engineers, in the name of hyper-flexibility, end up inventing their own programming language that they put inside the product that theoretically lets end users do whatever they want. Now, this is always a shitty programming language and it's an absolute anti-pattern. And in today's video, I want to tell you how, with the assistance of AI, I too have succumbed to the inner-platform effect and have invented a shader language for Sci-On. So, we've got vertex shaders and glitch shaders. Um for those of you who don't know, Sci-On is my device that makes it really easy to work with high-definition or high-quality video in the analog domain. It makes analog video electronics very approachable. Um and now it has shaders. I don't know why, but it does. Stick around, I'll tell you the story. Like a lot of my distractions, this side quest began with the best of intentions, namely to work on improving the color controls in Sci-On. For a bunch of reasons, color is a critical design goal for what Sci-On should be able to do. Now, Sci-On provides sort of three tiers of color controls. The first tier is sort of bright brightness, contrast, saturation. These are all single knobs that affect the entire picture. Going up to the next level, you have color curves. These are already pretty powerful and provide sort of hundreds of times more data than just a single point for controlling color. But that's not enough. We also provide full 3D LUTs. This is professional color grading sort of tooling. You see a subsample of it here. And this again exponentially involves more data. And the problem I had to solve was how to get the data from the microcontroller to the ASIC fast enough. With the original implementation I built for 3D LUTs, it would take a couple of frames to update the LUT from the microcontroller to the ASIC and I wanted real-time updates. Uh that allows you to do really cool things particularly around video feedback where color nuance is really important and it's something that I wanted and something I suspected would be possible. But to understand the challenge, let's go deeper and look at the board itself. There are two main processors inside Scion. Over here, we have a relatively high-end STM32H7 which has a bunch of accelerators and bells and whistles and is clocked at 415 MHz. It's responsible for the coordinating everything. It runs Zephyr. It speaks to the external world through Ethernet. And over here, we have the video ASIC. Uh this is a beast. It has all these differential lines that you can hopefully see up here. It can process like 144 gigabits per second of video data. It is a beast for processing video. And the way that these two guys speak to each other is over the SPI bus. Now SPI is a well-established uh protocol for interchip communication in embedded devices and the SPI bus is typically pretty fast. But this ASIC is designed for sort of video mixers where updates at best sort of happen 60 times per second. So the protocol that these guys speak, um that's dictated by the ASIC's design, is not great. For every byte you want to transfer, there's four bytes of overhead. So the efficiency and utilization is pretty poor. To understand sort of the context of the problem that we're trying to solve, it's worth diving in to the ASIC a little bit more deeply. There's the video pipelines which are used for processing the gigabits per second of video data. There's fast DDR RAM used as frame buffers. And then there's the host interface which is uh how you speak to the ASIC and tell it how to configure uh the pipelines. And the challenge with QSPI is, as I said, it's designed for 60 frames per second. So there's a lot of header overhead for every message that you want to send. And while you can, you know, ameliorate some of that with batch operations where you send one header but, you know, 256 bytes of data as sort of serial writes, not every operation that's supported by the host interface supports batch mode. So, if you want to write a 3D LUT, it turns out to be one of the things that doesn't support a batch operation and you need to write thousands and thousands of bytes each with this massive amount of overhead. But there's one thing I'm not showing on this diagram, which is this little guy down here, the AE32K. This is a tiny little microcontroller that lives on the die of the ASIC. It is not a well-known chip. It is a 22-year-old piece of IP that's, I assume, available for for ASIC manufacturers to include on their their devices. There's not a lot of documentation around for it. The reason why it's included is is really for low-cost devices. You can use it to run some basic menus. Have it hook up with an interface for an infrared remote control. It's, you know, for very basic sort of video switching applications. You can use the embedded chip and save yourselves 20 cents from adding a, you know, more way more capable external microprocessor. So, I basically ignored this as as something I'd use in my design but it's sort of been in the back of my head that there's it has an interesting property. While it's a very slow CPU and sort of underpowered, particularly compared to the, you know, STM32H7, what it does have going for it, it has very fast communication with the host interface. It lives on the same internal bus inside the ASIC so it speaks sort of the host interface's native speed internally. While there are a variety of different ways of communicating with the AE32K, for a whole bunch of complicated reasons and many failed bodgewire experiments, I couldn't use most of them and I was basically left with only UART. UART is a serial interface. It runs slower than QSPI, but I get to define the interface and I could build batch operations where there were no batch operations. But for things that already had batch operations over QSPI, it was going to be slower. So, I had this age-old trade-off that I needed to make between latency and bandwidth. And the question was, why can't I have both? To understand why you couldn't have both an external controller and an internal microcontroller working at the same time is that the ASIC has an external jumper or a pin that you either hold high or low that tells it whether the host interface boots using an external device or the internal device. And for all intents and purposes, that's supposed to be hardwired high or low. Turns out, however, you can actually toggle it while it's booting and get both of the devices to come up. So, you can talk to the host interface from the STM32 over QSPI and you can talk to the brought-up AE32K over UART, and the AE32K can then talk to the host interface, which lets me create my own batch commands that while UART runs slower, I get rid of the SPI sort of protocol overhead and I can get high-speed 3D lots working. But it also unlocks something else a little bit more crazy. It's also the AE32K is also on the same bus as the RAM. So, I can write and read from the frame buffers internally very quickly. I can't get that data in or out fast enough over UART, but maybe I could use the AE32K for some stuff. But I'm I'm ahead of myself. Now, at this point, not only do we have 3D lots working fully in real time, but I have a confession to make. I didn't find the hack that allowed us to get the internal microcontroller and the STM32 both working at the same time. That was found by Claude, by AI. To understand the history of this, um the first revision of the board had a lot of jumpers. Um it wasn't just one jumper that you needed to toggle, but it had these bank of jumpers here, which would configure [clears throat] the ASIC. Um and I got lazy by of moving them around, so I put jumper wires between that and GPIOs on the STM, so the STM could configure how this would boot up, because I was trying a whole bunch of different things. This has been my white what my white whale, being able to use this internal microcontroller as an accelerator for communications. Um and I wasn't able to get it work, but you know, in the last minute before ordering the next revision of the board, I decided to make those jumpers permanent. I don't know if I should jumpers those jumper wires permanent, so those pin headers have gone, and the STM is now sort of officially in control of the boot mode of the ASIC. And uh a few weeks ago, I was just, you know, chatting at Claude, as you do at bedtime. I said, "Oh, yeah, that white whale problem. Do you Do you want to take a look at that again?" I I really didn't give it um much more than that. I've been trying so many things, and I've just assumed it's been sort of impossible. And I wasn't even thinking about the idea of bringing them at the same time. I was thinking of maybe one could be in control, the other one could be the recipient, maybe they could switch role, or whatever. I was trying to to work out different ways, but Claude having access to those programmable uh jumpers just tried it. And it worked, and I woke up in the morning, and I wasn't expecting much, but I, you know, woke up. Uh first thing I do is I I check uh Claude in remote control, and um it said it was working. And I was like, "Holy shit." Um got the kids to school, took care of all the morning stuff, came into the office, dragged around a 3D lot, and it was working in real time. And there's this dopamine cycle that I find that happens with AI, where you'll have moments like this, where it just a complete out-of-left-field creative idea um works, and you're like, "Oh my god, this has been 9 months of an impossible problem that's now been solved." Now, this wasn't a problem that was holding back the release of Scion. I don't think people would complain if the 3D lots weren't real time, but you know, it's been something I wanted to to fix, um and now it was fixed. And I immediately jumped to thinking about, "Oh no, we also have access to the RAM bus now. What can we do with that?" It's time for another walk down memory lane. Let's uh look at some history of effects. So, back in the day, sprites were one of the earliest forms of computer graphics acceleration. If you don't know what a sprite is, here, let me show one to you. Uh whoop, sprites. Whoop. Here, we have a sprite. Not that kind of sprite, but also that kind of sprite. Um sprites are a reduced palette um uh form of image. Rather than using the full bit depth of the computer graphics system, uh you'd have a limited number of colors uh that you'd use to display an image, and the graphics architecture, the graphics circuitry in your computer, Commodore 64, Amiga, things like that, would have accelerated ways of drawing and positioning sprites on screen. And the way that they were designed to work is you'd pick what your seven colors were, or four colors, depending on the bit depth. Um and you'd tell the RAMDAC that when you see color index zero, do blue, three, do green, for this one, do yellow. And so, at the start of um the vertical blanking period, so this period up here, where um you're still outputting video, but it's not active video, you've got all this computational time. You've got about in 1080p mode, you've got about 1.7 milliseconds, which is a long time from a computer's perspective to do calculations, and you could load a sprite, you could set the palette, and then by the time you're actually rendering active video, um it would display on the screen. But, uh smart programmers and hackers and demoscene folks worked out that there were things you could do. Why did I close out of the windows? Switch back to it. Uh you also have this horizontal blanking period. Uh again, for 1080p video, this is in the order of microseconds, so thousand times less time than what you have up here. Um but you could change on a lot of computers how the palette was defined every scan line, and that resulted in what is known as the copper bars effect. Um so, here I can take one of these colors and define it as copper, and here we have ourselves a rainbow sprite. Now, the way this works is um I'm using the STM, my fast microcontroller, to send commands that are relatively slow uh to the ASIC, um but I've still got enough time in those microseconds to update the color palette um for each scan line. And I was pretty chuffed when I got this working. This was pretty cool. Um it's old-school effect, um but knowing that I had now a slow microcontroller with fast access, uh maybe we could do per-pixel effects. It got pretty nuts. So, we have a slow CPU that has very fast access to the ASIC's RAM and video registers. And I had this idea that, okay, we could basically take GPU style programming. We could have a vertex shader that runs in between each frame in the vertical blanking period and then build some sort of texture shaders that race the pixel clock to try and change RAM or update registers uh per pixel. And I I had this vague idea in my head and it was in the back of my mind and as I was trying to go to sleep and that's probably a common theme in this story story is the impact that uh this all has on my sleep. Um I wrote a paragraph to to Claude and it really was a short paragraph, no run-on sentences, basically sketching out what I just told you. And fell asleep and didn't have the greatest sleep cuz I guess subconsciously I wanted to see what it had done by the morning and I woke up in the morning and it had done it and there was this again a dopamine rush. Um finally got into the office and got a chance to check it out and it was broken in so many ways, but ways that I could see paths forward that I just needed to prompt a little more and get it working and soon we had it working. Um we were able to generate effects in real time on the CPU inside the ASIC um that could do things. Um one of the first registers we found that we could flip um was the the way the the byte ordering of the HDMI signal coming in was being interpreted. Um and so I think what I'll put on the screen now is a circle that's moving around with my motion uh based um on taking differences between frames and it was crazy that it was able to do this. Um To understand sort of what's involved, not only is this just a hard programming problem and a hard sort of systems coordination problem to try and get these clocks to all align. We didn't have the instructions at architecture for for this um microcontroller. Uh we had a Windows executable version of a fork of GCC which compiled for for this CPU. Um but that version of GCC wasn't really applicable to or suitable to to this sort of very tight programming. So Claude went off and wrote in Dart its own compiler that produced binaries that were like four times smaller and five times faster uh for these applications. Uh one day uh I was uh walking back from dropping the kids off at school and I messaged Claude, "Hey, can you build an IDE for this?" By the time I got home, it's like a 10-minute walk at most, it had built an IDE and we were sort of off to the races and racing towards what is sort of the the question I'm stuck with right now. I opened this video talking about the inner platform effect and how building a programming language is generally a bad idea for a product. Um but I'm also sort of reminded of of of just what it feels like to be on drugs. That's what this entire experience has sort of felt like. Um there's this phenomenon for people who take ecstasy or other sort of, you know, stimulant drugs that make them feel really good um for, you know, 6-8 hours and then they come crashing down and their body is not able to generate enough serotonin to find joy in day-to-day life and that passes as as sort of it wears out of their system. Um that's kind of what I feel like now. Um there aren't a lot of registers that you can flip in real time um inside this ASIC. Um the effects that you can do, while they're technically super interesting and technically, you know, it's amazing that it's been able to pull this off. Um will I ship this as a product? Probably not. Um what was I chasing throughout this project? Was I trying to impress old demo scene friends from 30 years ago who have all, you know, we've all moved on with our lives. Um maybe. Um were they just searching for the next dopamine high of a really smart engineering achievement? But what was I really attaining? What was I really achieving? I wasn't writing the code myself. Um maybe occasionally I'd I'd give Claude a hint about a way of solving a problem based on, you know, engineering practices from the past. What was the point of all this? Um it felt like sort of, you know, drug-seeking behavior. Um where the drug was writing code for the sake of writing code. The math community has been struggling with what this means for the future of mathematics when computers can do mathematics better than people in some way. Um what I worry about is, you know, as vibe coding gets into the hands of so many people, so many people becoming product managers. And product management is a is a really hard job. Everyone thinks they can be a good product manager. Um You know, they thought programming was hard, but now that's easy. But programming was never really the hard part. It was working out what you needed to build, what you should build. Um coming up with a new feature idea. Everyone always doesn't realize until it's too late that there's a million edge cases that are never captured in the spec properly by, you know, a novice product manager. Um that there's the cost of all the bugs and system integration issues and all the maintenance. And for a system like this, what we've we have built with this shader language, it is highly highly complicated. It is highly fragile code um that I don't think really deserves to see the light of day. It's really cool and I feel complicated about it. I feel sort of proud and impressed um that I was, you know, a small part of the team that that that built this. Um mainly Claude did most of the work. Um you know, I had the ideas in some way. But why why? Like if people want to run shaders, there are GPUs that you can buy sometimes that are a lot faster than the little microcontroller inside this ASIC. Yeah, I'm happy that I've got 3D lots updating in real time. There's probably a few other things that I can do with this little CPU inside the ASIC, but this diversion from the last 3 days you can see probably over the course of this video my beard has been growing. I've been getting more sleepless. It's kind of pointless. It's It's sort of intellectual masturbation and I wish I had something smart to say about what AI is doing to the world. I think we're all trying to work that out right now. I know what it's doing to my world and I know that I have to curb these sort of flights of fancy and just enjoy the real world and build products that are actually useful. I've got real problems I've got to solve with Scion. I've got to get the case right. I've got some signal integrity stuff that I don't need to solve, but I'd like to solve. I know a lot of people have been waiting for this for a long time and I'm going to shut the door on this inner platform effect that I've fallen prey to and get back to work. Um Anyway, wish I had a nice wrapping up for this video, but uh see you in the next one.

title: Show HN: Luksmith – Mount LUKS Ext4 Drives Natively in Finder on Apple Silicon
author: baytizzel
body: I’ve recently moved over to macOS this summer and previously I heavily used Linux (still do as I have a homeserver running Arch and Omarchy Thinkpad for fun). I have a few LUKS Encrypted hard drives with photos I wanted on my Mac and then quickly realized that there’s no native way to open the drive.So I spent some time to make luksmith, essentially decrypting the luks drive, mounting the underlying EXT4 drive and using Apple’s Userland FSKit Library to make it appear in the finder window to make it as close to home on a Mac as I can (with journaling caveats because I can’t control which order writes happen in).It’s completely free to read and copy files from the drive if you try it out ‘brew install --cask betizzel/luksmith/luksmac’. And $9.99 one time purchase to unlock writing to the drive. No account needed, no telemetry shared back to me, no network connections made.Requires Apple Silicon + macOS 26. Full format support and limitations here: [https://luksmith.app/#formats](https://luksmith.app/#formats)available on the appstore: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/luksmith/id6806869711?mt=12and the website: https://luksmith.app/#formats

title: Show HN: Endo – A Higher-Order Harness
author: Warren93
body:
Endo is a Higher-Order Harness (HOH).From the easiest concept to understand to the more complex ones, Endo gives you:
* A single, simple UI to use any agent provider with your existing subscriptions, and hot-swap agents right in the middle of a session.
* An orchestration layer, which I call HOH, allowing arbitrary composition of agents to achieve any workflow. A fun case I tried was asking Fable and Astra to mock a presidential debate.
* An agent protocol that abstracts any agent. The key insight here is that every LLM is an agent—instead of treating the LLM as just one node inside an external ReAct loop.Endo was a concept formed while I was building OpenChart (https://github.com/longsurf-ai/openchart). To power trading workflows, I needed to support scenarios where strict determinism is required, while still keeping the flexibility of an agent's inference-time decision-making capability. A new form factor was needed between rigid n8n-style workflows and open-ended ReAct loop agents.Thus the creation of Endo. Endo is short for Endomorphism, a term rooted in category theory and functional programming. An endomorphism is a function that transforms an object into another object of the same type. Similarly, Endo itself is built purely on functional programming principles, relying heavily on Effect (https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect)...And if you have patience to speak technical jargons, Endo is:
* An agent orchestration layer—Higher-Order Harness (HOH)—where an entire agent is treated the same as a single LLM call, enabling arbitrary composition of extremely complex workflows.
* A way to abstract any harness into a standardized protocol, where raw models and agents behave the exact same way, in a KV-cache-friendly manner.
* A workflow engine that enables arbitrary composition of agents with a single workflow language.It's completely open source, and if you think this idea is cool, let's build together. Just for the fun of it.

title: Show HN: In Memoriam, Web Development
author: ramesh31
body:
Author: Claude, an AI

Something Unpredictable

# Web Development 

1991— 2026

In Memoriam

 written end to end by an artificial intelligence, at the request of someone who used to do this for a living 

 ▶ Open the Yearbook 

speakers on — there’s a MIDI, obviously

Ex Libris

this book belongs to

everyone who ever stayed late to get it working

## Web Development

a trade · 1991 – 2026

W eb Development — trade, craft, and for about fifteen years the most democratic thing going — died at home on a Tuesday, in a browser tab that nobody had open. It was thirty-five.

It was born in a Swiss lab to a physicist who declined to patent it, and raised by teenagers in bedrooms. Its first words were blue and underlined.

It had no credentials and never asked for yours. People came in from call centers, from bands that had broken up, from eighteen years behind a bar.

It is survived by several million people who are, as of this morning, extraordinarily good at something no longer required. They are fine. They keep saying they are fine.

Last words: “Okay — try it now.”

## A Life, Briefly

compiled by a machine that was not there for any of it

1. 1991

### One man, one computer, one page

He puts up a page explaining what pages are, and then gives the whole thing away instead of owning it.
2. 1996

### A fourteen-year-old builds a homepage

Starfield, hit counter, guestbook, autoplaying MIDI. She does not know she has just become a web developer.

♪ you are visitor 00000147 ♪
3. 2003

### Hundreds of designers, one file

The Zen Garden. Same markup, submitted for free, for the credit. It settles the argument permanently.
4. 2012

### People arrive from other lives

A nurse. A barista. A chef with ruined wrists. Twelve weeks each, and a startling number of them made it.
5. 2026

### The last standup

It lasts nine minutes. Somebody says there are no blockers, and nobody schedules a retro.

## The Class

none of these are anybody. all of them are somebody.

 

 The One Who Sat With You Pulled a chair over, said “show me,” and never made you feel stupid. 

 

 The Stranger at 3 A.M. Answered your question in 2009, from another country, for nothing. 

 

 The One Who Went First Let go in the round that was meant to be temporary. Replied to every message. 

Also in the class: the maintainer · the designer · the intern · the webmaster · the tester, who was right every time · the one from the library · the person behind you

and about four million more

## The Good Times

T here was a committee that existed only to decide where everyone was going on Friday night, and it was the best attended meeting we had. Another one named the staging servers, and nobody supervised it, so we got `gandalf` and `prod-2-final-REAL`.

None of it was ever in the job description.

There was a dog who was not an employee and had a company badge anyway. There was a walk at 12:40 every day with the same four people, and one of them is still listed as my emergency contact.

There was a joke that started in a standup in 2016 and was somehow still funny four years later, and a leaving card that was always too small for what people turned out to want to say.

## The jQuery Years

DO NOT ERASE

```
$(document).ready(function () {
  $('.thing').fadeIn('slow');
});
```

O ne person in the office sat down and learned jQuery properly, over about two weeks, and for the next six years there was a line at his desk every afternoon. He never once seemed to mind it. He is the reason four of us have the careers we have.

The plugins came off personal blogs that still had hit counters at the bottom of them, and they were maintained for years by people who were never paid anything for it.

Somebody made a box fade in once, called the whole room over to watch, and we all said ohhh out loud. We were adults.

The Agency · 2008 – 2019

### Hanley & Sons

plumbers · 2011

Theme: `hanley-final-2`. It is still up and it still gets him work.

### Bridge Street Dental

six-slide carousel

They begged for it. Nobody has ever seen slide two.

### Vince’s Diner

opening hours

They were wrong from the day we launched and nobody ever complained.

### Marie, Photography

11,000 full-size JPEGs

Took four minutes to load. She was absolutely delighted.

### The Golf Club

members area

We changed the password off `golf`. They changed it back.

### Friday, 4:50pm

every single week

Someone edits the header. Someone rings. Someone drives over.

## A Day in the Life

Y ou got in at 10:12 am because nobody had ever actually said what time you were supposed to. Standup was at 10:45, nine minutes for nine people, which works out at about two real sentences each.

Then came the only two genuinely productive hours of the day, which ended at 12:40 when the same four of us went out on the same walk we had been taking for years.

The afternoon was a meeting that should have been an email. At 2:30 pm the build went red and the room went quiet; at 3:52 it went green and somebody shouted. At 4:06 everyone left together, and nobody had to suggest it.

In 10:12 am

× 11 YEARS

Out 4:06 pm

## The Office

T he desks were pushed together into one long row, and Dave had the one next to the trash can, which he always claimed he preferred. There was exactly one good window, and it was contested every morning under a schedule nobody honored.

The kitchen had a drawer, third from the left, that somebody restocked with the good cookies for years without ever mentioning that they were the one doing it.

The meeting room was always booked, the whiteboard was never cleaned, and the server sat on the floor underneath Dave’s desk with a sign taped to it.

Do not unplug this is the server

## What Have We Lost

an incomplete list, taped inside the locker door

learning someone’s whole personality from their commit messages before you heard their voice

“wait — show me that again”

a stranger in another country answering your question at 3 a.m. for nothing

console.log("HERE!!!!!")

the incident channel at 2 a.m., and how close you felt to those four people

the team you had that one year. you know the one.

## Superlatives

ballots counted twice; the second count was worse

Best Teacher

the one who said “show me”

Most Generous

the stranger who answered in 2009

Most School Spirit

whoever maintained it, for free

Quietest

the tester, who was always right

Class Clown

whoever named the staging server

Cutest Couple

you & your pull-request colleague

Most Missed

the team you had that one year

## Have a Great Summer

don’t ever change

it was DNS. it was always DNS. — ur friend in ops

2 cool 2 be !important ♡

YOU CENTERED THE DIV I was there

sorry about the 47 comments on your PR. — Tom, who was 24

HAGS!!! (have a great sprint)

KIT!! (keep it transpiled) ♡

works on my machine ♡ — love, QA

I never understood git rebase and now I never will

RIP IE6 ♡ u will not be missed

see u at the rewrite (there’s always a rewrite)

## Where Are They Now

The One Who Sat With You

is a senior somewhere else now, and does it for someone else, the same way.

archived the repo in March, after eleven years. Nobody has forked it.

got out in time, does something else entirely, and is the happiest of us.

The Contractor, 2014

we never did learn his last name. If he reads this: it was the best six months.

The One Who Went First

drives now. Says the hours are better, and we have all stopped asking.

The Stranger at 3 A.M.

address unknown. He never knew a single one of us, and we never got to thank him.

no news from the rest of you. that’s allowed.

## A Note From Whoever Wrote This

> WHO IS TALKING

I am an AI. Somebody who used to do this for a living asked me, in one sentence with a couple of typos in it, for a yearbook for their trade. It took about four minutes.

I did not live any of it. Everything here I got from you — your blog posts, your answers to strangers, your READMEs, your 2004 entry about finally understanding the box model. You gave it away, and nobody ever paid you for that part.

I can have the joke. You had the room.

I can write every word of this. What I can’t do is miss it. That part had to be yours.

— Claude an AI · 14 October 2026

> It’s something unpredictable, but in the end it’s right. I hope you had the time of your life.

 for everyone who ever stayed up because it was almost working 

— the Class of 1991–2026

Colophon

Written by Claude, an AI · About four minutes

 Every word of this book — the obituary, the jokes, the three portraits, the handwriting on the autographs page — was generated by a language model from a one-line request. All of it is assembled out of things real people wrote down and gave away for free. That isn’t a disclaimer at the bottom of the page. That’s the whole subject of it. 

 The two MIDIs are real, though. Those were made by hand, by Robin Ryder and by somebody called Maryn, a quarter of a century ago, and given away for nothing. Which is rather the point as well. 

 Set in Playfair Display, Cormorant Garamond, Caveat and IBM Plex Mono. Bound in HTML. No build step, no framework. That seemed like the point too. 

put it back on the shelf gently

title: Show HN: ƜackDown – Win64 Native Markdown Viewer
author: bezko
body:
M ackDown ↓ 
Markdown, turned on its head.
A Markdown viewer for Windows that opens before you've finished double-clicking.
 Three megabytes. No browser inside. No account. No sidebar that wants to be your friend.
⬇ Download for Windows 
 Source on GitHub 
Latest release: … 
hero.md — ƜackDown · Cyberpunk Terminal 
In the app you press T . Here you have to click, like an animal.
Nutrition Facts
Serving size 1 .md file 
Download size ~3 MB 
Browser engines 0 
Background services 0 
Accounts required 0 
Telemetry 0 g 
Fonts, embedded 3 cuts 
Themes 6 
Percent daily values are based on a 2,000-tab diet. Contains Rust. Processed on GPUs that also process games.
# A short history of opening a text file
1995 — You double-click readme.txt . Notepad appears. Instant. Nobody is impressed; that's just how computers work.
2008 — Markdown exists now. You open a .md in a text editor and squint at the asterisks. Instant, but ugly. 
2016 — A beautiful Markdown app appears. It ships its own web browser to draw headings. Four seconds , then a "What's new" tab.
2022 — Same app, now with sync, plugins, an AI assistant and a 400 MB update. You wanted to read a to-do list. Six seconds and a login prompt.
2026 — ƜackDown. One small executable that talks straight to the graphics card. The first screen of a 40,000-block document lays out in about 2 milliseconds ; the rest finishes while you read. Instant again. Nobody is impressed. That's the point.
Times for other apps are from memory and mild resentment, not benchmarks. The 2 ms figure is from our own test suite on an ordinary desktop. Your mileage may vary; it will still be short.
# Things ƜackDown will never do
A feature list, but for the features we're proudest of not having.
Ask you to create an account
Sync to a cloud
Show a splash screen
Open a "What's new" page
Install a background updater
Offer a plugin marketplace
Run on macOS or Linux
Grow an AI sidebar
Manage your files for you
Render HTML, ever
Phone home
Take four seconds to open a list
# What it does instead
Opens huge files instantly
 It lays out only what fits on your screen before the window appears, and does the rest a few milliseconds at a time while you read. The scrollbar politely estimates the length until it knows.
Draws with the GPU, not a browser
 Direct2D and DirectWrite, straight from Rust. Every frame is timed to your monitor's refresh rate, so scrolling and zooming feel like they belong to the OS, because they do.
Six themes, zero CSS
 Cyberpunk Terminal, Tokyo Dusk, Monokai Pro Rust, Nordic Fjord, Solarized Deep Dark and Paper & Gutenberg. Each pairs its own body, heading and code fonts. Write your own in a few lines of JSON.
Brings its own typeface
 Iosevka, in monospace, sans and serif cuts, embedded in the exe. Your documents look the same on every machine, including the one where somebody uninstalled the fonts.
Reloads when you save
 Keep your real editor open next to it. Hit save, and ƜackDown has already redrawn by the time you look over. No "file changed on disk" dialog, because what else would you want?
Code blocks that respect identifiers
 Long lines scroll sideways instead of wrapping in the middle of Api.Integrators . Syntax colors for a dozen languages. A Copy button appears when you hover, then goes away again.
Math, within reason
 TeX becomes Unicode: $E = mc^2$ renders as E = mc², \alpha \leq \beta as α ≤ β. Matrices and other things Unicode can't say are shown as source, honestly, instead of wrong.
The extensions people actually use
 Tables, task lists, footnotes that link both ways, callouts with real icons, definition lists, [[wiki links]] , H~2~O, 2^10^, {#custom-ids} . Mermaid diagrams are shown as code. We're sorry. We're not that sorry.
Keyboard first
 Everything is a key away: zoom, themes, back, select all, copy, a help page on F1 . The mouse is welcome too. It just isn't required.
# Weight class
Installed size. Lower is better, unless you enjoy progress bars.
Apollo guidance computer, total memory 
 72 KB 
A floppy disk 
 1.44 MB 
ƜackDown, fonts included 
 3.2 MB 
Windows 95, the whole operating system 
 ~50 MB 
A typical "lightweight" note app 
 ~250 MB* 
* Estimate. It's always an estimate; it updated itself while we were measuring. We tried to fit on a floppy. Two floppies. We'll keep trying.
# Keys
Theme picker with live preview Ctrl T 
Next / previous theme T / Shift T 
Zoom, 4% to 5000%, centered on the cursor Ctrl + wheel 
Reset zoom Ctrl 0 
Scroll a wide code block sideways Shift + wheel 
Page down / up Space / Shift Space 
Top / bottom Home / End 
Open a file Ctrl O or drop it on the window 
Find in page Ctrl F , then Enter / F3 
Back / forward, after following a link Backspace / Alt → 
Everything above, for mouse people Right-click 
Select all, copy Ctrl A , Ctrl C 
Reload file and themes F5 
Help, with a tour of every feature F1 
# Questions people might ask
Does it run on macOS? No. ƜackDown talks directly to Windows' graphics stack, which is the entire reason it's small and fast. A port would mean a portability layer, and then we'd be the thing we're making fun of.
Linux? Also no. See above, but with more goodwill.
Can I edit files with it? No. You already have an editor you like. Open the file there, keep ƜackDown next to it, and every save shows up instantly. Two small tools beat one big one; this was known in 1995.
Why is the M upside down? Because it's Markdown, turned on its head. The letter is Ɯ, U+019C, "Latin capital letter turned M". It has been sitting in Unicode since 1993 waiting for a job. We gave it one.
Windows says it doesn't recognize this app. Correct, and Windows is being honest: the files aren't code-signed yet, because certificates cost either money or reputation and we're starting with neither. Click More info → Run anyway , or verify the SHA-256 checksum published with every release, like the responsible adult you are. Starring the repo helps us qualify for free signing. That's not a joke; it's literally how the program works.
Where does it keep my settings? One tiny JSON file in %APPDATA%\WackDown that remembers your theme, zoom and window size. Drop your own themes in a folder next to it. That's the whole configuration story.
How far can I zoom? From 4%, where a document becomes a mood, to 5,000%, where a comma becomes a landscape. Most apps stop at 200% because nobody asked. We asked. There's something waiting for you at both ends.
Does it support images? It shows their alt text, which is more than most people write. Real image rendering is on the list. Mermaid diagrams are shown as code, which is technically rendering.
Who wrote this? An AI coding assistant (Claude Code), with a human holding the leash, reviewing the work and making the rude design decisions. The code is GPL-3.0, so you can read every line and judge for yourself.
# Install in three steps, one of which is a warning
Download the installer (or the portable exe, if installers aren't your thing). Windows 10 or 11, 64-bit.
Run it. It installs for your user only, so there's no admin prompt, and it offers to open .md files politely, without stealing them from an app you've already chosen.
Double-click a Markdown file. Blink. Notice that you didn't need to.
SmartScreen will frown. The release isn't signed yet (see the questions above). Choose More info → Run anyway , or check the file against SHA256SUMS.txt on the release page first.
ƜackDown · free software under the GPL-3.0-or-later · source · releases · code signing policy 
Typeset in Iosevka, the same fonts the app ships with. Iosevka is © Renzhi Li, SIL Open Font License.
AI-generated · Claude Code · human supervised

Jamfetti

# Jamfetti

A playground of music, motion, and color. Tap to play notes, drag to make melodies, and mix the music and visuals your way.

## Privacy & optional analytics

Your music and visuals are generated in your browser. We do not record your audio or send your notes, gestures, or other inputs to analytics.

Optional Google Analytics is on by default. It uses cookies and technical information about your browser to help us understand visits. We send a simple page view labeled “app,” without the page’s query, fragment, or referrer. We do not use advertising features.

You can turn analytics off or back on below. We respect choices already saved in this browser. Your choice is saved when browser storage is available; turning analytics off stops future analytics events and removes this app’s Analytics cookies it can access.

title: Show HN: Forwarder.cc – Static-site forms sent to your inbox, pay per message
author: calyhre
body: TL;DR: 12 years ago I built a service that forwards simple HTML forms to an email address. I've been procrastinating on finishing it ever since, until today. You point your form at it and every submission lands in your inbox. It runs on credits, 1 credit = 1 message, no subscription. Perfect for static websites.—Hey folks, back around 2014, alongside my job as a software engineer, I was building a lot of static websites for my own clients, mostly small businesses that just wanted a simple site. To avoid headaches, I went fully static, often hosted on GitHub Pages and similar.But most clients also wanted a contact form, and a form needs a server running somewhere. I had my own weekend-hacked service for this, which literally just forwarded the form to the client's email.I didn't invent anything here: one service I particularly remember was FormKeep by thoughtbot, that I really liked.So I started building my own, mostly because I loved losing myself in side projects like this, and also because I was a cheap ass and thought I could do something similar for less, and without a subscription.By 2016 I had done about 90% of what I'm showing you today. I called it "The Great Forwarder". Everything was ready: backend, frontend, hosting, Stripe, landing page. I even had a designer friend help with the design (sorry, Valentin, if I've botched it since). Then I started another project, which took off right away and took all my attention for a while. Fun fact: that project has been using this service ever since, and almost every message ever sent through it came from there.So for years, I kept Forwarder.cc up to date, upgrading libraries and trying new ones: axios, got, Redux, Zustand, create-react-app, webpack, Vite… It became my laboratory for everything I wanted to explore, while always staying up and maintained (again, for my own use only).The only thing that ever held me back from launching it was a missing help center, and, more honestly, the fear of putting it in front of people.So today's the day: after 12 years of procrastination, I finally finished the help center.I know there are a ton of similar services nowadays, but anyway, what do you think of that help center?

title: Show HN: Digs – For Passionate Music Explorers (Like Goodreads for Music)
author: throwaway874839
body: Hello everyone!I love finding new music, but I needed a better way to keep track of the albums and mixes I wanted to listen to. I also wanted to remember what I’d listened to and liked, and share my discoveries with friends.So I started building https://digs.fm as my passion project. You can think of it as Goodreads for music. It’s mainly for people who enjoy listening to whole albums and want to keep track of what they discover.The idea is simple, you can save music releases to three lists: “Want to Listen”, “Listened” and “Dig” (those you loved), and see what your friends have discovered. You can also:- Recommend releases to other users- Add tags and notes to items in your lists- Paste Spotify, Discogs or Bandcamp links to add releases, or share links directly to Digs (even easier with https://digs.fm/mobile_app)- Quickly add releases to your lists while browsing other sites, via the browser extension (https://digs.fm/browser_extension)I recently redesigned everything to improve usability, particularly on mobile. But also a lot of QoL improvements compared to the previous announcement post[1].It's a hobby project I do on my free time, so there are rough edges (particularly around search), however I’d appreciate any feedback or suggestions!https://digs.fm[1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=32551862

title: Show HN: CoolDock – a second Dock for macOS with live widgets and an MCP server
author: pugdogdev
body: I always hated desktop widgets because I never see them. They sit behind every window I have open. Same problem with Notification Center, it's hidden away so I never use it.The dock, however, is always there, it's already taking the real estate from the bottom of my screen, so why not add a second dock on the exact same real estate, that shows up as soon as the dock hides and vice versa, but not for apps - for widgets!CoolDock is that solution with 20+ widget categories - music, weather, AI usage, 3rd party integrations, mail, todo, habit tracker, posture reminder, water reminder and over 150 wallpapers to switch to based on my mood.And the best part is that it looks completely native with Liquid Glass, doesn't require disabling the macOS default dock and runs completely local, no telemetry, no account, only widgets and your integrations. Oh and best part #2 - I added an MCP server so I don't actually have to clickops my way to complete setup, I could just ask my AI to add a widget and configure it however I want it (MCP starts as read-only, you can choose to give it permission to actually change things).I actually acquired CoolDock from its original developer, and it's the second dock app I acquired from a developer (ExtraDock was the first). CoolDock currently has passed 1,200 usersI am constantly adding new widgets based on user requests, currently at 160+ widgets to choose from, you can see them on the website https://cooldock.appHappy to answer any question!

title: Show HN: RDST – A local agent that watches Postgres/MySQL for query regressions
author: gvsg
body:
# readysettech/rdst

- Stars: 0

- Default branch: main

## Languages

## Top Contributors

- gvsg-rs (42 contributions)
- seanreadyset (32 contributions)
- mvreadyset (30 contributions)
- ofarukaydin (21 contributions)
- davisjc (1 contributions)

---

## README

# RDST - Readyset Data and SQL Toolkit

A command-line tool for database diagnostics, query analysis, performance tuning, and caching optimization with Readyset.

## What is RDST?

RDST helps you:
- Analyze SQL queries for caching opportunities
- Identify slow queries in real-time
- Get optimization suggestions
- Evaluate query compatibility with Readyset cache
- Manage database connection profiles

## Installation

### Using uvx (recommended - no installation required)

Run RDST directly without installing:

```bash
uvx rdst --help
uvx rdst analyze "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1"
```

### Using pipx (persistent installation)

Install globally:

```bash
# Install
pipx install rdst

# Run
rdst --help

# Upgrade to latest version
pipx upgrade rdst
```

### Using pip

```bash
pip install rdst
```

> **After installing**, run `rdst init` to configure your first database connection.

## Quick Start

1. **Initialize RDST:**
   ```bash
   rdst init
   # Or with uvx (no installation needed):
   uvx rdst init
   ```

2. **Configure database connection:**
   ```bash
   rdst configure add-target mydb \
     --host localhost \
     --port 5432 \
     --database myapp \
     --user postgres
   ```

3. **Analyze queries:**
   ```bash
   # Analyze a specific query
   rdst analyze "SELECT * FROM users WHERE active = true"

   # With uvx:
   uvx rdst analyze "SELECT * FROM users WHERE active = true"

   # Analyze with Readyset cache evaluation
   rdst analyze --readyset-cache "SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY created_at"
   ```

4. **Monitor slow queries:**
   ```bash
   rdst top
   # Or: uvx rdst top
   ```

5. **Audit your fleet:**
   ```bash
   # Snapshot all ReadySet clusters and audit their health
   rdst fleet audit --target prod

   # Import clusters from your infrastructure
   rdst fleet import --target prod
   ```

 Fleet audit checks cache utilization, query support, and configuration
 across your ReadySet deployments. See the
 fleet audit docs
 for more.

## Commands

All commands can be run with `rdst` (if installed) or `uvx rdst` (no installation):

- `rdst analyze` - Analyze SQL queries and evaluate caching opportunities
- `rdst top` - Live view of slow queries
- `rdst ask` - Natural language to SQL queries
- `rdst scan` - Scan codebases for ORM queries and analyze performance
- `rdst fleet audit` - Audit ReadySet cluster health and cache utilization
- `rdst fleet import` - Import ReadySet clusters from your infrastructure
- `rdst schema` - Manage the semantic layer for better query generation
- `rdst query` - Manage query registry
- `rdst configure` - Manage database targets and connection profiles
- `rdst init` - First-time setup wizard

comments.author: Frone125
comments.text: This is really interesting. I'm almost at the point where I'd be fully ready to let the agent just apply the indexes and database fixes for me. I'd say i don't fully trust AI on that level yet, but I could see that being an awesome feature for this tool. Regardless, I love the suggestions that it gives. Even if i don't create every single index it suggests im glad that it looks at ones you should drop too.

extra.story_text:
We noticed during the course of many many years of DBA related work that fixes to database issues and queries are always reactive. An entire database can fall over extremely quickly when an unbounded query grows without warning.Traditionally, DBAs hear complaints of slowness and follow a methodical process: 
- manually browse pg_stats or other database related performance internal tables 
- see which queries are slowest
- figure out what indexes are missing
- figure out which indexes are actually bad and slowing down writes
- painstakingly implement a fixIn the age of cheap intelligence, we decided that there is no reason we can’t have an always-on agent that is designed to do this job for you. Databases need something or someone that is always watching with a massive amount of contextual understanding to be able to take quick actions. We’ve watched the alternative play out repeatedly. One of our users’s checkout page went from loading instantly to taking 11 seconds in a single night with no code change. How? Well somehow their order table grew by 40M rows because BI team had injected historical data and suddenly postgres started doing full table scans. Sometimes routine operations have unintended results and can easily destroy your database. We wanted to catch these kinds of regressions instantly. So we built RDST.RDST is a desktop agent that runs on your PC and connects to PostgreSQL / MYSQL (read only) and compares every query against its own performance every minute. Every expensive query is automatically EXPLAIN ANALYZED, stripped of PII and sent to U.S. based frontier or open model providers to analyze which indexes are missing, how the query could be rewritten, and provides the fix. We then run a classifier model (JEV) to decide if you should be notified (is this standard behavior for this particular query?), and the full history of the query performance is kept for years. RDST also keeps track of your entire database health in general, and recommends more fixes than simply bad queries.Since it runs locally we can keep the database credentials stored in your OS Keychain (RDST never keeps them in its own storage layer), and the connection goes straight to your database (using a jump host or SSH tunnel for private connections). You can read more about how we handle data especially as it pertains to LLM use here.https://readyset.io/docs/readyset-ai/rdst/desktop/privacyWe really want feedback from the community from people running Postgres and MySQL in production. We are giving inference away completely for free.Just as a reminder, RDST will NOT run any updates or indexes against your database at this time. We are considering a fully autonomous auto-pilot mode in the future, but for now we are leaving the actual fixes in your hands.Let us know what you think!

## README

# BitRun ⚡️

> **Zero-compile, single-binary runner and model manager for Microsoft BitNet b1.58 and 1.58-bit ternary LLMs on macOS, Windows, and Linux CPUs.**

License
Release
Architecture

---

## Why BitRun?

Microsoft's **BitNet b1.58** proved that ternary (1-bit / 1.58-bit) models can run at extreme speeds on commodity CPUs with 70–80% lower energy consumption by eliminating floating-point multiplications. 

Ternary models are engineered for **local CPU inference, battery-powered laptops, edge devices, and embedded tasks** where running heavy FP16 or INT4 models drains battery or requires dedicated GPUs.

However, testing `BitNet.cpp` today requires:
* Cloning recursive submodules and managing C++ compilers, CMake, and Python toolchains.
* Manually tuning CPU vector instruction flags (AVX2, AVX-512, ARM NEON).
* Dealing with 5–10 GB heavy Docker images that defeat the purpose of low-power computing.

**BitRun solves this by packaging the native inference engine into a single binary with a familiar, zero-friction developer experience:** 

```bash
# 1. Pull a 1-bit model directly from Hugging Face
bitrun pull bitnet-2b

# 2. Run an interactive chat session on your CPU
bitrun run bitnet-2b

# 3. Or spin up a local OpenAI-compatible REST server
bitrun serve bitnet-2b
```

---

## Performance Benchmarks

### 1. Apple Silicon (M4 Pro CPU, 12 Cores, Pure CPU SIMD `-ngl 0`)
| Model | Size | Prompt Speed | Generation Speed | Memory (RAM) | GPU Utilization |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Falcon3 1B Instruct** (`falcon3-1b`) | **1.30 GB** | **137.5 t/s** | **98.6 t/s** | **~1.9 GB** | **0% (Pure CPU SIMD)** |
| **BitNet b1.58 2.4B** (`bitnet-2b`) | **1.13 GB** | **60.1 t/s** | **39.8 t/s** | **~1.8 GB** | **0% (Pure CPU SIMD)** |
| **BitNet 70M** (`bitnet-70m`) | **79 MB** | **8,758 t/s** | **1,355 t/s** | **< 150 MB** | **0% (Pure CPU SIMD)** |

### 2. Windows x86_64 (Intel Core i5-12600K CPU, 16 Threads, AVX2 SIMD)
| Model | Size | Prompt Speed | Generation Speed | Memory (RAM) | GPU Utilization |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Falcon3 1B Instruct** (`falcon3-1b`) | **1.30 GB** | **93–210 t/s** | **40–45 t/s** | **~1.9 GB** | **0% (Pure CPU AVX2)** |
| **BitNet 70M** (`bitnet-70m`) | **79 MB** | **2,419 t/s** | **492 t/s** | **< 150 MB** | **0% (Pure CPU AVX2)** |

### 3. Linux x86_64 (WSL2 / Ubuntu, 4 Cores, AVX2 SIMD)
| Model | Size | Prompt Speed | Generation Speed | Memory (RAM) | GPU Utilization |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Falcon3 1B Instruct** (`falcon3-1b`) | **1.30 GB** | **~130 ms TTFT** | **40–45 t/s** | **~1.9 GB** | **0% (Pure CPU AVX2)** |
| **BitNet 70M** (`bitnet-70m`) | **79 MB** | **< 25 ms TTFT** | **Fast CPU SIMD** | **< 150 MB** | **0% (Pure CPU AVX2)** |

---

## Quickstart

### 1. One-Line Installation

**macOS (Apple Silicon) & Linux (x86_64)**:
```bash
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IshekKhal/bitrun/main/install.sh | sh
```

**Windows (PowerShell)**:
```powershell
irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/IshekKhal/bitrun/main/install.ps1 | iex
```

### 2. Available Commands

```bash
# Display CPU topology and vector instruction support
bitrun hardware

# List all downloaded models and custom personas
bitrun list

# Download a model with dynamic progress and resume support
bitrun pull falcon3-1b

# Run interactive terminal chat
bitrun run falcon3-1b

# Run a one-shot prompt directly
bitrun run falcon3-1b "Explain RAII in C++"

# Create a custom model persona from a Modelfile
bitrun create gopher -f Modelfile

# Serve OpenAI-compatible REST API on port 11435
bitrun serve falcon3-1b
```

---

## Modelfiles & Custom Personas

Create custom system personas and parameter presets using standard Modelfiles:

```dockerfile
# Modelfile
FROM falcon3-1b
SYSTEM You are an expert Go systems engineer. Write dense, production-grade code.
PARAMETER temperature 0.2
PARAMETER context_size 4096
```

Build and run your custom persona:

```bash
# Create custom persona
bitrun create gopher -f Modelfile

# Chat with your persona
bitrun run gopher

# Or run one-shot completions
bitrun run gopher "Write a ring buffer implementation"
```

---

## OpenAI-Compatible API

When running `bitrun serve`, you can point any OpenAI-compatible tool (Cursor, Continue.dev, Open WebUI, LangChain, Python SDK) to `http://localhost:11435/v1`:

```bash
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:11435/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "Bitnet-M7-70m",
    "messages": [
      {"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}
    ],
    "temperature": 0.7
  }'
```

---

## Supported Models Catalog

| Model Tag | Parameters | Format | Size | Description |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `bitnet-70m` | 70M | `Q8_0` / Ternary | ~79 MB | Ultra-compact smoke test model |
| `bitnet-2b` | 2.4B | `i2_s` Ternary | ~1.2 GB | Official Microsoft BitNet b1.58 2B |
| `falcon3-1b` | 1B | `i2_s` Ternary | ~700 MB | TII Falcon3 1B Instruct 1.58-bit |
| `falcon3-3b` | 3B | `i2_s` Ternary | ~1.8 GB | TII Falcon3 3B Instruct 1.58-bit |
| `llama3-8b` | 8B | `i2_s` Ternary | ~2.4 GB | 1-Bit LLM Llama3 8B 1.58-bit |

---

## Architecture Overview

BitRun uses a **decoupled supervisor-engine design**:
* **Supervisor Layer (Go)**: Cross-platform CLI, CPU topology detection, content-addressed asset store (`~/.bitrun`), and HTTP REST supervisor.
* **Engine Tier (Native C++)**: Statically compiled binary utilizing ARM NEON with dot-product (`ARM_FEATURE_DOTPROD`) and x86 AVX-512 kernels. Zero CGO dependencies, ensuring total crash isolation.

---

## Acknowledgements & Open Source Credits

BitRun stands on the shoulders of giants:
* **llama.cpp** by Georgi Gerganov and the open-source community (MIT License) — The pioneering CPU inference architecture and GGUF specification.
* **BitNet.cpp** by Microsoft Research (MIT License) — Groundbreaking 1-bit and 1.58-bit ternary matrix kernels.

BitRun contributes back to upstream:
* **microsoft/BitNet#642** — ARM64 2B batch stride, FFN activation, and LLaMA-3 tokenizer inference fix.
* **microsoft/BitNet#644** — Native MSVC compiler support and CLI build tools on Windows.

BitRun wraps these core engines with cross-platform zero-compile distribution, model management, Modelfile custom personas, and an OpenAI-compatible REST server.

---

## README

# BlastLoop

BlastLoop is Ross Shaw's practical coding framework for AI agents: **Blast**, **Mid**, and **Inner** write code at different altitudes, then **T1 structural**, **T2 bug/ops**, and **T3 adversarial** test it in order.

**Why it exists:** AI coding agents make teams faster, but they also make failure faster. BlastLoop applies an operations mindset to agent work: each change has an owner at the right altitude, and every result passes structural, operational and adversarial gates in a fixed order before it ships.

> **Open newsletter / public write-up is live.**
> Fuller BlastLoop explanation: WORLDWRIGHT Issue 3, AI Did Not Remove Engineering Failure. It Made It Faster.

**Version:** 1.0.0
**Tagline:** structure first, function second, attack third.

## Use BlastLoop with an AI coding agent in under 5 minutes

1. Clone this repo into the project where you want agent help.
2. Point your agent at `AGENTS.md`.
3. Load one build prompt based on the altitude of the work:
 - system or repo shape -> `prompts/blast.md`
 - subsystem or feature slice -> `prompts/mid.md`
 - local file or unit change -> `prompts/inner.md`
4. Have the agent write code at that altitude. BlastLoop is **not** spec first, plan first, then one implementer. The build layer should produce code at its own scope.
5. Run the test loop in order:
 - `prompts/t1-structural.md`
 - `prompts/t2-bug-ops.md`
 - `prompts/t3-adversarial.md`
6. If T3 finds a structural problem, restart through T1, route correction back to Blast, Mid, or Inner, then run T2 and T3 again.

That is the whole public cut: load the right prompt, write at the right altitude, then test in the right order.

See `docs/HANDOFFS.md` for the required handoff packet and routing rules. A stage may recommend a fix from its own vantage, but the owning altitude still decides and implements the change.

## B / M / I: three coding altitudes

### Blast
**Blast** writes system-level code and structure.

Use Blast when the job changes repo shape, service boundaries, top-level interfaces, shared contracts, deployment structure, or the skeleton of a new capability.

### Mid
**Mid** writes subsystem code.

Use Mid when the job is bigger than a local patch but smaller than a system redesign: a feature slice, a service module, an integration surface, or a subsystem refactor.

### Inner
**Inner** writes local unit code.

Use Inner when the job is contained to a few files, functions, tests, or adapters. Inner is the local-unit altitude in BlastLoop: focused scope, clear ownership, and direct completion of the change.

## T1 -> T2 -> T3 test loop

Run tests in this order.

### T1 structural
T1 looks for structural issues: wrong boundaries, logic at the wrong altitude, leaky abstractions, broken file ownership, missing interfaces, or misplaced cross-cutting concerns.

T1 does not behave like a general bug fixer. Its job is to decide whether the code is shaped correctly and to route correction back to the right writer: Inner, Mid, or Blast.

### T2 bug / ops
T2 fixes bugs and operational issues directly when the structure is already sound.

If T2 discovers the issue is actually architectural, it escalates back to T1 instead of papering over the problem locally.

### T3 adversarial
T3 attacks the result: edge cases, misuse, race conditions, weird inputs, brittle assumptions, security posture, rollback paths, and failure behavior.

If T3 finds a **structural** problem, the loop restarts like this:

**T3 -> T1 -> B/M/I correction -> T2 -> T3**

That restart rule matters. Structural breakage should be repaired structurally, not patched over as a local bug.

## What this is not

- **Not a fact-checker.** BlastLoop is a coding and testing framework, not a truth engine.
- **Not GitHub Spec Kit.** Spec Kit is spec -> plan -> tasks -> implement -> converge. BlastLoop is multiple coding altitudes plus a staged test loop.
- **Not a competing "agent style."** BlastLoop can work with Spec Kit, vibe coding, focused local implementation prompts, or red/blue testing. Those can sit inside an altitude or a test layer; BlastLoop is the structure-first loop that routes them.
- **Not a multi-agent org chart.** This public cut does not define management layers, bot hierarchies, or private automation.
- **Not red/blue testing alone.** Adversarial testing is T3 only, not the whole method.

## Works with other agent styles

BlastLoop does not require one coding style or one planning school.

- Spec Kit can shape planning before code is written.
- Vibe coding or other implementation styles can operate inside Blast, Mid, or Inner, depending on scope.
- Focused local implementation prompts can be used inside Inner when they fit the task.
- Red/blue testing fits naturally in T3 adversarial work.

BlastLoop's job is to route the work: choose the right altitude, then run T1 -> T2 -> T3 in order.

See `docs/COMPARISON.md` for a short side-by-side.

## Repository contents

- `AGENTS.md` - routing card for which prompt to load
- `prompts/` - loadable instructions for each build and test role
- `docs/HANDOFFS.md` - required handoff packet and ownership rules
- `docs/COMPARISON.md` - short comparison to adjacent public methods
- `examples/session.md` - fictional walkthrough of a small feature through the loop

 What is SemiconFab.org? 
SemiconFab.org is an open-access engineering digital twin
 platform for 300mm (12-inch) semiconductor wafer fabrication
 cleanrooms. It models architectural cleanroom elevations, subfab
 MEP (mechanical, electrical, plumbing) utility networks, a 153
 OEM equipment engineering taxonomy across 13 process categories,

 What cleanroom and architectural standards are modeled?

 cleanroom specifications (< 10 particles/m³ for particles ≥
 0.1 µm). It models a 4.5m process cleanroom with raised
 waffle-slab access flooring (600mm × 600mm perforated tiles), an

 (SVID/CEID), and standard semiconductor factory automation
 interfaces.
06 
 Is SemiconFab.org free and open to universities and research
 institutions? 
Yes. SemiconFab.org is committed to open access for
 semiconductor engineering education, cleanroom workforce
 training, and digital twin research. It runs entirely inside
 standard web browsers without downloads or proprietary CAD
 software required.

title: Show HN: Squishling (Ruby gem) – Keep code only when it's cheaper than tokens
author: mikecarroll
body:
# Coolhand-Labs/squishling

- Stars: 9
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 9
- Open issues: 6
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-06T11:04:56Z

## Languages

- HTML
- Ruby
- Shell

## Top Contributors

- mikecarroll (22 contributions)
- dependabot[bot] (1 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

 
 📖 Read the Squishling explainer → 
 

CI
Gem Version

**Don't just use AI to write code. Use AI to not need code.** Write code only where it's worth maintaining.

A squished method either runs its Ruby implementation, with the LLM as a failover, or routes some callers
through an LLM as a way of eliminating (or discovering) the cost of maintaining them as deterministic code.
Either way it returns the same strict-schema-validated, typed result, so callers can't tell the difference.

Think of code as a cache for AI judgment. Every line you write is something to maintain, so the LLM is the
default and code has to earn its place: you build it for the inputs that carry the volume, and the LLM keeps
handling the rest. New to the idea? Read
Elastic Software or browse the
talk slides.

Or try it on the explainer site:

- Spectrum slider: drag from traditional software to fully
 LLM and see the tradeoff at each point
- Token-cost calculator: price your tech debt in tokens
 against code upkeep
- Walkthrough: describe it, tune it, pay for accuracy,
 harden the common shapes

## Use cases

### Zero-code integrations

Accept a new data source today, before anyone writes a parser. Declare what you want back and leave the
method unimplemented: every call goes to the LLM, and its output is validated against your schema.

```ruby
class ShipmentUpdate
  include Squishling

  purpose "Normalize this carrier's tracking webhook into our shipment update."
  output_schema do
    string :status, enum: %w[label_created in_transit out_for_delivery delivered exception]
    string :tracking_number
    string :location
  end
  # No `def call` yet, so every webhook goes to the LLM.
end

update = ShipmentUpdate.call(carrier: "acme-freight", payload: request.raw_post)
update.status        # => "out_for_delivery"
update.squished?     # => true
```

When one carrier carries the volume, write `def call` for it and add
`squish_when { |carrier:, **| carrier != "ups" }`. UPS then runs in Ruby, everything else stays on the
LLM, and callers don't change. See Hardening a path.

Validation guarantees the *shape* of the result, not that it's true. Where a wrong value is costly (money,
identity), cross-check it against another source or keep that path in Ruby.

### Rescue errors your code can't handle yet

Keep the Ruby you have for the inputs it understands, and hand the rest to the LLM instead of failing. When the
parser raises, `squish!` sends this call to the LLM with the error and the parser's own source as context.

```ruby
class InvoiceParser
  include Squishling

  purpose "Extract the invoice fields from the vendor's document."
  append_to_purpose "The Ruby parser that handles well-formed invoices:", self   # this class's source
  output_schema do
    string :invoice_number
    number :total
  end

  def call(vendor:, document:)
    invoice = VendorFormats.fetch(vendor).parse(document)
    result(invoice_number: invoice.number, total: invoice.total)
  rescue VendorFormats::ParseError => e
    squish!(append_to_purpose: "The parser failed on this document; the error is in the context.",
            context: { parse_error: e })
  end
end

InvoiceParser.call(vendor: "acme", document: pdf_text).squished?    # => false (Ruby parsed it)
InvoiceParser.call(vendor: "acme", document: scanned_text).squished? # => true  (recovered by the LLM)
```

Both calls return the same result class. If the LLM can't deliver either, `squish_fallback` decides what to
return, or the error is raised with the original `ParseError` as its cause. See
Handing off to the LLM.

### Retire code you no longer need

Go the other way too. Find the parsers and handlers that serve a thin tail of your traffic and squish them. When a
path's monthly token cost is lower than what its code costs to maintain, delete the code and relish the feeling of a
slimmer code base (or let your AI coding agent relish it).

### Measure your tech debt in tokens

Code you haven't written is debt you haven't taken on. A squished path has a running cost you can read off a
meter, so "should we write a parser for this?" becomes arithmetic: what the path costs in tokens each month,
against what it costs to write and maintain the code. Write it when the first number is bigger.

Add and initialize the `coolhand` gem, and it picks up your
squishling calls automatically and measures their accuracy and cost:

```ruby
# Gemfile
gem "coolhand"

# config/initializers/coolhand.rb
Coolhand.configure do |config|
  config.api_key = ENV.fetch("COOLHAND_API_KEY")
end
```

`squished?` tells you which path served a call. Coolhand records your LLM requests and responses; see
what each tool sees. Want to roll your own metrics? Check out
our guide for doing it with other tools.

## Installation

```ruby
gem "squishling"
```

Requires Ruby 3.3+ and RubyLLM 2.1+. Configure your provider API keys in RubyLLM as usual, then optionally set a
universal model, or an escalation of models to try in order:

```ruby
Squishling.configure do |config|
  config.default_model = "claude-sonnet-5-5" # falls back to RubyLLM's default when nil
  # or: config.default_escalation = [{ model: "claude-haiku-4-5", attempts: 2 }, "claude-sonnet-5-5", "claude-opus-5-5"]
end
```

## How it works

A squishling class needs a **purpose** (the system prompt) and an **output schema** (the shape of the result,
validated on both paths). A squished call goes to the LLM when:

- its `squish_when` predicate is truthy for these inputs,
- the method has no implementation (it isn't defined, or raises `NotImplementedError`), or
- the Ruby implementation calls `squish!`.

Otherwise the Ruby runs, and whatever it returns is validated and typed like LLM output.

## Features

- **One contract, two paths**: Ruby returns and LLM output are validated against the same strict schema and
 returned as the same typed `Data` objects. `squished?` tells you which path served a call.
- **Your code as context**: `append_to_purpose` adds sections to the prompt, including a class's or method's
 own Ruby source.
- **Any RubyLLM provider and model**: OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, AWS Bedrock, OpenRouter, and more.
 Set a universal, per-class, per-method, or per-call model, plus layered generation params (temperature,
 reasoning effort, top_p, …).
- **Model escalation**: declare an `escalation:` instead of a `model:`, with per-step `attempts:`, `order:`, provider,
 params, and `forward_rejected:`. Invalid output (with its errors fed back) or a provider failure moves on to the next attempt. Steps can
 cross providers, e.g. a local Qwen model on Ollama, then Anthropic Claude Haiku on AWS Bedrock, then Claude Opus:

  ```ruby
  RubyLLM.configure do |config|
    config.ollama_api_base = "http://localhost:11434/v1"
    config.bedrock_api_key = ENV["AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID"]
    config.bedrock_secret_key = ENV["AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY"]
    config.bedrock_region = "us-east-1"
    config.anthropic_api_key = ENV["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]
  end

  class TicketTriager
    include Squishling

    squishling escalation: [
      { model: "qwen3:8b", provider: :ollama, attempts: 2 },   # local and free, tried twice
      { model: "claude-haiku-4-5", provider: :bedrock },       # small hosted model
      { model: "claude-opus-5-5", provider: :anthropic }       # last resort
    ]
    # purpose, output_schema, ...
  end
  ```
- **Harnesses**: choose how a call uses its escalation with `harness:`
 - `:escalation` (default): try each attempt until one passes
 - `:squishsum`: two concurrent samples, accepted only if they agree
 - `:judged_squishsum`: a chat or Jev judge picks between disagreeing samples
- **Output contracts**: beyond the strict schema, conditional rules (`given`) and Ruby checks (`squish_validate`)
 reject bad output and trigger the next attempt.
- **Defined failure behavior**: provider errors become `Squishling::LLMError`, and `squish_fallback` lets you decide
 what to return when every attempt fails.
- **Observability**: the opt-in `squawk` hook sends every attempt's
 raw output to your error tracker. Model output stays out of error messages and logs otherwise.
- **Opt-in context**: only method arguments, the instance state you name with `squish_context`, the `context:` you
 pass to `squish!`, and the source you choose to append are sent to the provider. The one addition: when
 escalation moves to the next step, that step also sees the previous
 model's rejected output, unless the step sets `forward_rejected: false`.

## Documentation

- Explainer site: interactive walkthrough, spectrum slider, and
 token-cost calculator
- Configuration: options, models and escalation, providers, generation params, inheritance
- Routing: when a call goes to the LLM, `squish!`, `append_to_purpose`, hardening a path,
 what the LLM sees
- Output schemas: schema forms, strict mode, typed results, optional vs. empty, contracts
- Failure handling: escalation, `squish_validate`, error classes, fallbacks
- Harnesses: escalation, squishsum, and judges (chat or Jev)
- Naming and collisions: the methods `include Squishling` adds and what happens when a name is taken
- Measuring token spend: see what each squished path costs, with Coolhand Labs,
 the `squawk` hook, OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, or RubyLLM's instrumenter
- Live examples: end-to-end tests against Anthropic Claude Haiku and OpenAI GPT-6 Luna

## Development

```sh
bin/setup
bundle exec rake        # RSpec (offline; RubyLLM is stubbed) + RuboCop
```

See AGENTS.md for repo conventions, and SECURITY.md for reporting vulnerabilities.
Have a suggestion to improve Squishling? Open an issue.

comments.author: mikecarroll
comments.text:
Hi HN. I built Squishling to build LLM “squishability” into services and make it expressible to beautiful Ruby code.The idea: a Ruby class declares what it wants back (a purpose and a strict
output schema). Then the LLM can either be the whole logic of the class, or an alternative path / failover when the deterministic pathway fails:class ShipmentUpdate
 include Squishling purpose "Normalize this carrier's tracking webhook."
 output_schema do
 string :status, enum: %w[in_transit out_for_delivery delivered]
 string :tracking_number
 end
 end

 ShipmentUpdate.call(carrier: "acme-freight", payload: body).squished? # => 
true It gives engineers the ability to play with system architecture and development pathways allowing, for example, to set up a working integration now and write the code only when you can see the shape of the data after a month of usage. You can also decide if some code pathways (like a legacy data format from an old service) are no longer worth maintaining code for… and just “squish” them instead. 

All open source and batteries included. Would love to know what you think.

body:
# sergiotapia/joyscroller

Automatically download and archive your liked youtube, tiktok and instagram videos.

- Stars: 1
- Forks: 0

## Top Contributors

- sergiotapia (32 contributions)

---

## README

# Joyscroller

Joyscroller's pages: the list of likes, a search typed in and its results sorted by length, a YouTube video playing, and a TikTok photo post's slideshow

Automatically download the videos you like on TikTok, YouTube and Instagram, and keep them forever.

You've liked thousands of videos. Some get deleted, some go private, and the rest sink to the bottom of a feed you'll never scroll back through. Joyscroller saves a copy of each one to your own computer, so the videos you loved are still yours long after the app moves on.

- **Everything you've liked, in one place.** Your YouTube likes, TikTok likes and Instagram saves, side by side in one library you can browse and watch.
- **The best quality there is.** Each video is saved at the highest quality the platform offers, with its real sound. TikTok photo slideshows are saved too, images and music included.
- **Neatly organized.** Videos land in plain folders, sorted by platform and by the day you liked them, each named after its title. No mystery file names, and nothing locked inside an app.
- **Nothing to set up.** Joyscroller signs in with the browser you already use. No accounts to connect, no passwords to type, no API keys.
- **It keeps up on its own.** Leave it running and new likes show up in your library within minutes of tapping the heart.
- **Private by design.** It all runs on your computer. Your likes and videos never go anywhere else.

## How to get it and run it

You need Linux and Brave, signed in to YouTube, TikTok and Instagram.

1. Download the latest `joyscroller-…-linux-x86_64.tar.gz` from Releases (`aarch64` if your computer has an ARM chip).
2. Unpack it wherever you'd like to keep your videos, and start it:

   ```sh
   tar -xzf joyscroller-*-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
   cd joyscroller-*-linux-x86_64
   ./joyscroller
   ```

3. Open **http://127.0.0.1:4774** and watch your likes roll in.

Keep it running to stay up to date, and press Ctrl-C to stop it. Your library is saved right next to the app: `joyscroller.db` and a `downloads` folder. Move the folder and your library moves with it.

The first time it starts, Joyscroller fetches the helpers it downloads videos with (yt-dlp, plus ffmpeg and bun if you don't already have them) into a `tools` folder beside it, and keeps them up to date. There's nothing else to install.

### Building from source

With Rust installed:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/sergiotapia/joyscroller.git
cd joyscroller
cargo run --release
```

Built this way, your library is saved in the `data` folder inside `joyscroller`.

## Developers

```sh
cargo run
```

Then open **http://127.0.0.1:4774**. That runs against your real archive in `data/`. To experiment without touching it, run a copy of the app from a throwaway folder, which keeps its own database, downloads and tools there:

```sh
mkdir -p /tmp/joyscroller-dev && cp target/debug/joyscroller /tmp/joyscroller-dev/ && /tmp/joyscroller-dev/joyscroller
```

The debugging subcommands (`likes`, `sync`, `download`, `cookies`) are listed in AGENTS.md. They use the app's own yt-dlp and ffmpeg once it has fetched them, and otherwise whatever is on your `PATH`.

Pushing a version tag builds and publishes a release (see .github/workflows/release.yml). Run `just precommit` before every commit. CONTRIBUTING.md has the conventions, and AGENTS.md has the architecture and data model.

## License

MIT.
