comments.author: burnrate
comments.text: Hey great question! WebContext owns an output buffer (i.e., RenderBuffer) that components write HTML into directly, avoiding intermediate allocations and copying. It needs to be mutable for this reason. This is one of the key ways we're able to make Proa the fastest server-side rendering engine on the market.By default, WebContext composes RenderBuffer (but it can be overriden via generics) which uses fixed-size 4 KiB pages. When a page runs out of room, it adds another page without moving the HTML already written. This avoids copying the accumulated output during growth! Its designed to be a performance improvement over Vec<u8>For context, the problem with Vec<u8> is that every time a vector reaches maximum capacity, it has to reallocate a new area of memory (typically 2x larger than the previous allocation) and then copy everything into that new buffer. This adds a ton of overhead, especially if you're writing large pages.Checkout https://github.com/Proa-Labs/proa/blob/384136f87fc9f91747477... if you're curious about RenderBuffer's design

comments.author: burnrate
comments.text: Hey! Author of Proa here, thanks for checking it out! The idea is to just accelerate the time it takes to create components, similar to Shadcn or other component libraries. You can create a new component and modify them however you like. It’s nice because they have both the WebRender and MdRender trait implemented, and saves you a bit of time. Also for slightly more complex components like Calendar, we’ve crafted the component with all the JS interactivity required to do things like switch months, select start and end date, etc

comments.author: burnrate
comments.text: I can't speak for the others as I am not as familiar with how they're engineered, but with Proa I spent a painstaking amount of time to try and move as much of the work to compile time as possible and being really careful about how memory is allocated. And a lot of those small improvements add up over time!

comments.author: burnrate
comments.text: I highly recommend! I've been writing Rust professionally for 5 years now. Compile times are slow but I love the language. https://cheats.rs/ is a resource i go back to often in case you're interested in learning more. Especially since as you get more into it, Rust has a lot of weird types like RefCell and Cell and OnceCell and disambiguating between them is a chore sometimes. Hope it helps!

comments.author: burnrate
comments.text: Thank you so much, that's very kind of you! Sounds great! Please feel free to provide any feedback or ways I can make it better for you.

comments.author: burnrate
comments.text:
> This might be a silly question, but why 2 views for html and markdown?No such thing as silly questions! Yes there are cases where it can be inferred from one to the other, but in many cases you may want to be very specific about how you author the markdown view. I'll give you a few examples:1. Custom components: For example, let's say you have a carousel component. It's not really straightforward to infer the markdown from this. But you probably want the carousel to render as a series of markdown image tags. A custom view would be helpful for this. Same goes for Calendars, SVG charts, Diagrams, form inputs, tabs, popovers, and more.2. Information omission: Agents don't need all of the information on your page. For example, a dark/light button... probably doesn't need a markdown equivalent. But a button that is an anchor tag that links to another page, probably you should keep. So having the ability to custom author the markdown render target based on the data it's rendering is helpful.One of the unique aspects of Proa's authoring model is that it supports composability of Markdown components, just like JSX, which is I think one of its standout features. And you can embed native control flow (if, loops, match, etc.) directly in the md!{} macro just like you could with JSX. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pJx84jdBDKU&t=21s explains it quite well if you're interested. Makes the readability and code ergonomics much much better.> it's exciting to see so many rust web frameworks popping up but I'm in total decision paralysis.I am a bit biased here but I think Proa is the most complete framework currently for building a production web application in Rust. I know its newer and doesn't have as many stars, but maybe I can point you to three things to see if it gives you more confidence:1. Data loading: https://proa.so/docs/framework/data-loading
2. Browser interactivity: https://proa.so/docs/rsjs/signals (all in rust btw)
3. Security: https://proa.so/docs/framework/security-headersProa, Proa UI, latency.so, and a few other sites are all using Proa in production. It's the fastest SSR framework in production (https://github.com/Proa-Labs/proa-benchmarks) and supports streaming SSR (checkout the streaming SSR benchmark), suspense, etc. And it's server framework agnostic so you can use it with actix, axum, and other frameworks if you want.

title: Show HN: Ghx – A caching proxy for GitHub CLI, built for AI agents
author: brunoborges
body:
⚡ ghx 
Features 
 How It Works 
 Install 
 gh Shim 
 Agent Plugin 
 Security 
 Docs 
GitHub
⚡ Built for AI agent workflows
Stop hitting
 GitHub rate limits 
A caching proxy for the GitHub CLI that makes repeated commands instant.
 Singleflight coalescing means 10 agents asking the same thing triggers just 1 API call.
Get Started 
 View on GitHub 
Why ghx?
🚀
10x Faster
Cached responses return in ~0.1s instead of ~1s. Your scripts and agents feel instant.
🔄
Singleflight Coalescing
Five agents requesting the same PR list simultaneously? Only one API call is made. All five get the result.
🎯
Allowlist-Based
Only known-safe read-only commands are cached. Mutations pass through directly and invalidate related cache entries.
🔌
Drop-In Replacement
Just use ghx instead of gh . The daemon auto-starts. No configuration needed.
📊
Built-In Dashboard
Real-time web dashboard shows hit rates, per-command stats, and a live request log. Helps you tune your TTL.
🛡️
Safe by Design
Context-aware cache keys prevent cross-repo collisions. Unix socket with strict permissions. No tokens stored.
How It Works
Agent 1
ghx
Agent 2
ghx
Agent 3
ghx
IPC
ghxd
daemon
Cache 
 Singleflight 
 Metrics 
exec
gh
GitHub CLI
1
You run ghx pr list 
The ghx client resolves your repo, branch, and auth context, then forwards the request to the ghxd daemon over a Unix socket.
2
Daemon checks the cache
Using a context-aware key (repo + branch + host + auth + args), it looks for a valid cached response. If found and within TTL, it returns instantly.
3
Cache miss? One execution only
On a miss, the daemon executes gh once. If other clients request the same thing concurrently (singleflight), they all wait for and share the single result.
4
Response is cached and returned
The stdout, stderr, and exit code are cached with a configurable TTL (default 30s). The client writes stdout/stderr and exits with the original exit code.
Real-World Performance
Measured with gh pr list --repo cli/cli --limit 2 --json number,title 
Without ghx (direct gh) 1,129 ms 
1.1s
With ghx (cache hit) 105 ms 
0.1s
Live Dashboard
Monitor cache performance at http://localhost:9847/ 
JSON API
The dashboard data is also available as JSON for scripting and automation:
curl http://localhost:9847/api/stats | jq . ⎘ 
 curl http://localhost:9847/api/log?limit=50 | jq . ⎘ 
 curl http://localhost:9847/api/ttl-analysis | jq . ⎘ 
What Gets Cached
Only explicitly allowlisted read-only commands are cached. Everything else passes through.
Command Cached Notes 
gh pr list/view/status/checks/diff ✓ Cached With any filter/format flags 
gh issue list/view/status ✓ Cached Including --json , --comments 
gh repo view/list ✓ Cached 
gh run list/view ✓ Cached 
gh workflow list/view ✓ Cached 
gh release list/view ✓ Cached 
gh search repos/issues/prs/commits/code ✓ Cached 
gh api (GET) ✓ Cached REST GET only 
gh label list ✓ Cached 
gh gist list/view ✓ Cached 
gh project list/view ✓ Cached 
gh cache list ✓ Cached Actions cache 
gh ruleset list/view/check ✓ Cached 
gh org list ✓ Cached 
gh pr create/merge/close ✗ Mutation Invalidates PR cache 
gh issue create/edit/delete ✗ Mutation Invalidates issue cache 
gh auth/config/codespace ✗ Passthrough Always direct to gh 
Custom Cacheable Commands
Add commands to the allowlist without recompiling. Edit ~/.ghx/config.yaml 
 and list subcommand prefixes under additional_cacheable .
 Any gh invocation whose arguments start with a listed prefix will be cached.
 Restart the daemon after making changes.
ttl: 60s
additional_cacheable:
 # Cache `gh status` output 
 - "status" 
 # Cache Actions variable listings 
 - "variable list" 
 # Cache team member queries 
 - "api graphql" 
Install
# Install with Homebrew (macOS) 
 brew install brunoborges/tap/ghx ⎘ 
 # Or one-liner (macOS / Linux) 
 curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brunoborges/ghx/main/install.sh | bash ⎘ 
 # Windows (PowerShell) 
 irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/brunoborges/ghx/main/install.ps1 | iex ⎘ 
 # From Source 
 git clone https://github.com/brunoborges/ghx.git ⎘ 
 cd ghx && make build ⎘ 
GitHub Releases
Pre-built binaries are available for macOS (Apple Silicon), Linux (x64 & arm64), and Windows (x64 & arm64).
 Browse releases → 
gh Shim for Transparent Caching
When you install ghx, a lightweight gh shim is automatically placed on your PATH
 if no existing GitHub CLI is detected. This is especially powerful for AI coding agents —
 they call gh by default, and the shim ensures every command is routed through the ghx caching layer
 before hitting the real GitHub CLI. No agent configuration needed.
1
Install ghx — a gh shim is created automatically
During installation (Homebrew, install script, or PowerShell), ghx checks if a real gh binary exists on your system. If not, it installs a tiny shim at gh that routes all commands through ghx .
2
Agents call gh — caching happens automatically
AI agents like GitHub Copilot and Claude Code use gh for GitHub API calls. With the shim in place, every gh pr list , gh issue view , or gh api call flows through ghx's cache — eliminating redundant API requests and preventing rate limits, with zero changes to the agent.
3
The real GitHub CLI is obtained on first use
If ghx needs the real GitHub CLI to execute a command, it automatically downloads and installs gh for you. No manual setup required — just run your commands and ghx takes care of the rest.
⚠️ Already have the GitHub CLI installed?
When a real gh binary is detected, ghx will not install the shim — so agents will keep calling gh directly, bypassing the cache. You have two options:
Option A 
Remove the GitHub CLI and reinstall ghx. The shim will be created, and agents automatically get caching via gh . ghx will download the real gh binary on first use.
Option B 
Keep the GitHub CLI and install the agent plugin instead. The plugin teaches agents to call ghx directly instead of gh .
Agents Plugin
For Claude Code and
 GitHub Copilot CLI —
 install the plugin and your agent automatically prefers ghx over gh .
1
Add the marketplace
/plugin marketplace add brunoborges/agent-plugins ⎘ 
2
Install the plugin
/plugin install ghx@agent-plugins ⎘ 
3
Agent learns to use ghx 
A built-in skill teaches the agent to prefer ghx for all GitHub CLI commands. Binaries are lazy-installed on first use — no manual setup needed.
Plugin Docs 
 Marketplace Repo 
Security
ghx is designed to be safe by default — no secrets stored, no network exposure.
🔒
Owner-Only Socket
The Unix domain socket uses 0600 permissions. Only your user can communicate with the daemon.
🔑
No Tokens Stored
Auth tokens are never written to disk or cache. Only a SHA-256 fingerprint is used in cache keys to prevent cross-account collisions.
🌐
Localhost-Only Dashboard
The web dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1 only — it is not accessible from the network.
💨
In-Memory Cache
All cached data lives in memory and is lost on daemon restart. Nothing is persisted to disk.
👤
Per-User Isolation
Each user runs their own isolated daemon instance. No shared state between users on the same machine.

title: Show HN: Swift Render – programmatic video with SwiftUI and Metal
author: Akashchandran
body:
# skyblanket/swift-render

Programmatic motion graphics in Swift — SwiftUI scenes + Metal shaders → MP4. A native Remotion alternative, built for the AI era.

- Stars: 3
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 3
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-05-21T00:41:00Z

## Languages

- Metal
- Python
- Swift

## Topics

- creative-coding
- macos
- metal
- motion-graphics
- programmatic-video
- remotion-alternative
- swiftui
- video-generation

## Top Contributors

- skyblanket (30 contributions)

---

## README

 

# swift-render

**Programmatic motion graphics in Swift. SwiftUI scenes + real Metal shaders → MP4.**

*The native-Apple answer to Remotion — built for the era where AI writes the motion graphics.*

CI
macOS 14+
Swift 5.10
Release
License: MIT

 

https://github.com/skyblanket/swift-render/raw/main/docs/assets/launch-film.mp4

> **The 55-second launch film above is one Swift file** (`LaunchFilm.swift`) — Timeline sequencing, springs, four live Metal shaders, 3D, an audio-reactive segment, and a synthesized soundtrack. Written by an AI, **3,450 frames rendered in 29 seconds** on a MacBook. Click ▶. Sound on.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/skyblanket/swift-render && cd swift-render
swift run swift-render render JustRenderIt --audio audio/jri.m4a --out out/ad.mp4   # ~7s later: a finished ad, sound included
```

---

## Why not just use Remotion?

Remotion is great — and it's React rendered by **headless Chromium**, frame by frame, screenshot by screenshot. swift-render is a different bet: render natively on the GPU-accelerated Apple stack, and make every frame a **pure function of time**.

| | **swift-render** | **Remotion** |
|---|---|---|
| Render engine | Native SwiftUI `ImageRenderer` | Headless Chromium screenshots |
| 1080p60 render speed | **~100–140 fps** (M-series) | typically ~15–30 fps |
| Animation model | `t: Double` → View. That's the whole API | `useCurrentFrame()` + hooks, refs, effect deps |
| Determinism | **Proven** — byte-identical re-renders, tested in CI | best-effort (browser, font, thread timing) |
| GPU shaders | **Real Metal** (`.colorEffect`, 12 shaders included) | WebGL/canvas workarounds |
| Typography | Native SF / CoreText, SF Symbols, full blend modes | Web fonts in a browser |
| Audio-reactive | Built-in offline FFT → `audio.band(.bass, at: t)` | `useAudioData` + visualization utils |
| Data-driven renders | `--props file.json` (Codable) | `inputProps` ✓ |
| Sequencing | `Timeline { Clip }` result builder | ` ` / ` ` ✓ |
| License | **MIT — free for everyone** | source-available; free ≤3-person companies, then $25/dev/mo ($100/mo min) |
| Install weight | Swift package, **zero dependencies** | node_modules + a Chromium download |
| Toolchain | `swift run`, done | npm, bundler, browser binaries |
| Runs on | macOS 14+ | anywhere Node runs ✓ |
| Web preview/player | ❌ render PNG/MP4 fast instead | ✓ Studio + ` ` — genuinely good |
| Render farm | your Mac (it's fast) | Lambda ✓ |

**Use Remotion** if you need browser embeds, a web player, or Lambda-scale farms.
**Use swift-render** if you want native quality, 5–10× faster local renders, real shaders, and an API a language model writes correctly on the first try.

## The whole API fits in your head

A scene is a pure function: time in, view out. No state, no timers, no animation races — and nothing for an LLM to hallucinate.

```swift
import SwiftUI

public struct Hello: RenderScene {
    public static let defaultDuration: Double = 3.0

    @MainActor public static func body(at t: Double, duration: Double) -> some View {
        let p = Ease.spring(t, from: 0, to: 1, response: 0.5, dampingFraction: 0.6)
        Text("hello.")
            .font(.system(size: 120, weight: .black))
            .foregroundStyle(.white)
            .scaleEffect(0.8 + 0.2 * p)
            .opacity(Ease.clip(t, 0, 0.4))
            .frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)
            .background(.black)
    }
}
```

Register it in `Sources/SwiftRenderCLI/main.swift`, then:

```bash
swift run swift-render render Hello --out out/hello.mp4
swift run swift-render frame Hello --at 1.2 --out out/check.png   # preview one frame in ~1s
```

### Sequencing — `Timeline`

No segment math, no frame counting. Clips get **local time**; transitions overlap automatically; pinned clips float over everything:

```swift
Timeline(t) {
    Clip(2.2) { local in TitleCard(t: local) }
    Clip(2.4) { local in SpringShowcase(t: local) }.transition(.slide(0.45))
    Clip(2.4) { local in MetalMoment(t: local) }.transition(.flash())
    Clip(4.0) { local in Outro(t: local) }.transition(.fade(0.5))
    Clip(at: 0, for: 9.9) { local in ProgressHUD(t: local) }   // pinned overlay
}
```

https://github.com/skyblanket/swift-render/raw/main/docs/assets/timeline-demo.mp4

### Springs — closed-form, scrub-safe

`Spring` is solved **analytically** (under/critical/overdamped) — position at any `t` is computed directly, never integrated. Scrub to frame 4081 and get the exact same pixels, every run. Plus `easeOutBack`, `elastic`, `bounce`, `expo`, `cubicBezier(…)`.

### Audio-reactive — `--audio`

The file is FFT-analyzed **once** before rendering (RMS + bass/mid/high envelopes); scenes read it as a pure lookup, so determinism survives:

```swift
public struct AudioBars: PropsAudioScene {
    public static func body(at t: Double, duration: Double,
                            props: Props, audio: AudioTrack) -> some View {
        let bass = audio.band(.bass, at: t)        // 0…1
        // scale, glow, slam on the beat …
    }
}
```

https://github.com/skyblanket/swift-render/raw/main/docs/assets/audiobars.mp4

> The soundtrack itself is generated by `tools/make_jri_audio.py` — kicks, whooshes and an 808 placed at the scene's exact timeline anchors. Audio and video can't drift, by construction.

### Data-driven — `--props`

```bash
swift run swift-render props AudioBars > p.json     # JSON template from the scene's defaults
swift run swift-render render AudioBars --props p.json --audio beat.wav
```

Pipe in JSON per record and render a thousand personalized variants — the AI/data-pipeline workflow Remotion's `inputProps` made popular, native.

## Sound, in Swift

Scenes declare their own soundtrack — same constants drive the cuts and the
hits, so audio/video sync is structural, not manual. The synth (kicks, claps,
hats, crashes, sub bass, risers, 808 booms, drones, whooshes — with two-bus
sidechain pumping) is pure Swift, deterministic, and renders a minute of audio
in ~0.1s:

```swift
public static func soundtrack(duration: Double) -> Score? {
    Score(duration: duration) {
        fourOnFloor(from: 2.4, to: 33.6)          // kicks + backbeat claps
        hatSixteenths(from: 2.4, to: 33.6)
        bassline([.a1, .a1, .c2, .g1], from: 2.4, to: 33.6)
        crashes(at: chapters)                      // the SAME array as the Timeline
        riser(at: 33.6, duration: 2.4)
        boom(at: 36.0)
    }
}
```

```bash
swift run swift-render render KineticType        # score synthesized + muxed, zero flags
swift run swift-render audio KineticType --out out/score.wav   # export the track alone
```

`--audio file` always wins over a scene's score. Audio-reactive scenes react
to their own synthesized score — declare the beat, and the visuals hear it.

## Real Metal shaders

Drop a `.metal` file in `Sources/SwiftRender/Shaders/` and `swift build` — shaders compile automatically (SwiftPM build plugin). Call them on any view:

```swift
Rectangle().fill(.black).colorEffect(
    ShaderLibrary.bundle(.module).galaxy(.float2(1920, 1080), .float(Float(t)))
)
```

Eighteen ship in three packs — `rimGlow`, `foilHolographic`, `plasmaField`, `chromaticAberration`, `audioBars`, `caustics`, `liquidMetal`, `kaleidoscope`, `truchet`, `galaxy`, `neonGrid`, `smokeFlow`, `warpTunnel` — plus the studio pack from the launch film: `metaballs` (raymarched chrome), `inkFlow`, `interference`, `voronoiInk`, `monoTunnel`:

https://github.com/skyblanket/swift-render/raw/main/docs/assets/shader-gallery.mp4

(If a `.metal` file is newer than the compiled metallib, the CLI warns you loudly — no silently-stale shaders.)

## Twelve aesthetics, one engine

Swiss, neo-brutalist, Bauhaus, synthwave, glassmorphism, terminal, art deco,
vaporwave, blueprint, stop-motion zine, fluid aurora, kinetic type — each one
~40 lines of Swift, chained by a live card-zoom transition, closing on all
twelve running at once:

https://github.com/skyblanket/swift-render/raw/main/docs/assets/style-reel.mp4

```bash
swift run swift-render render StyleReel --audio out/reel.wav
```

## More demos

| | |
|---|---|
| `LaunchFilm2` — the launch film: every feature, one file | `swift run swift-render render LaunchFilm2 --audio out/launch.wav` |
| `StyleReel` — 12 aesthetics with card-zoom transitions | `swift run swift-render render StyleReel --audio out/reel.wav` |
| `Kinetic` — 12s kinetic-typography reel: word slams, marquee, galaxy iris, odometer ring | `swift run swift-render render Kinetic` |
| `JustRenderIt` — the hero ad, beat-synced soundtrack included | `swift run swift-render render JustRenderIt --audio audio/jri.m4a` |
| `AudioBars` — audio-reactive + props reference scene | `swift run swift-render render AudioBars --audio audio/jri.m4a` |
| `TimelineDemo` — Timeline/transition/springs reference | `swift run swift-render render TimelineDemo` |
| `ShaderGallery`, `ShaderShowcase`, `TextReveal`, `CardStack`, `ParticleField`, … | `swift run swift-render list` |

https://github.com/skyblanket/swift-render/raw/main/docs/assets/kinetic.mp4

## CLI

```text
swift-render render <Scene> [--duration s] [--fps n] [--aspect 16:9|9:16|1:1]
                            [--audio file] [--props file.json] [--range a:b]
                            [--no-postfx] [--out path]
swift-render frame  <Scene> --at <t> [--out path.png]    fast single-frame preview
swift-render props  <Scene>                              print default props JSON
swift-render list                                        all registered scenes
```

## How it works

1. Your scene is `(t, duration) → some View` — pure, deterministic, `@MainActor`.
2. `Recorder` walks frames `0..<duration*fps`, renders each via `ImageRenderer`, pipes BGRA pixel buffers into `AVAssetWriter` (H.264), muxes audio with `AVMutableComposition`.
3. A global `PostFX` pass (film grain + vignette, seeded and deterministic) makes raw SwiftUI feel cinema-grade. Opt out with `--no-postfx` or own it per-scene with `ownsPostFX`.
4. There is no step 4. No browser, no server, no project file.

Determinism isn't a vibe — `swift test` includes a render-twice-byte-identical check, and CI runs it on every push.

## Use it as a library

```swift
.package(url: "https://github.com/skyblanket/swift-render", from: "0.5.0")
```

```swift
import SwiftRender

let recorder = Recorder(config: .init(fps: 60, size: .init(width: 1920, height: 1080)))
try await recorder.render(to: url, duration: 5) { t in MyView(t: t) }
```

## For AI agents

`docs/ai-quickstart.md` is a compact, LLM-ready guide to the whole API. The design goal: an agent that has never seen this repo writes a working, good-looking scene on the first attempt. (This README's hero ad is the proof.)

## Requirements

- macOS 14+ (Apple silicon recommended; that's where the speed numbers come from)
- Xcode 15+ toolchain (`xcrun metal` needed only when editing shaders)
- ffmpeg optional — handy for GIF/thumbnail post-processing

## Roadmap

- SwiftPM build plugin for automatic metallib compilation
- `contact ` grid-sheet export · transparent ProRes 4444 · 10-bit masters
- Audio-reactive FFT improvements (configurable bands, onset detection)
- Linux? No — this is proudly the native-Apple lane.

## License

MIT — see LICENSE.

## Contributing

See CONTRIBUTING.md. Scenes must stay pure functions of `t` — that rule is the product.

body: TLDR: I’m building Earshot - the sound detection app that can detect (ideally) any sound described by text.The neural model under the hood is a CLAP-style model (CLIP for audio): basically during the training you force the model make inner text and audio representations to match. And then you can use such model as 0-shot audio classifier. For POC I used LAION’s clap-htsat model but it turned out to be quite "heavy" so I’ve trained a smaller one by myself.As for text encoder I used model from the EfficientAT family; for audio I used jhu-clsp/ettin-encoder-32m. The training was performed on my mighty 2x1080 Ti home server. The trained weights can be found on my HF: https://huggingface.co/mirth/earshot-clap-mn10-ettin32I would appreciate it if you could test this application (especially if you could report if an app missed the sound).A couple of disclaimers:1. The sound never leaves you device.2. It can miss the sound so it’s not a replacement for your monitoring system (but an extra pair of ears).3. I’m aware that similar functionality is presented in the Apple HomePod but there is a minor difference: to add very custom sound for detection on HomePod you need first to record it (to train inner HomePod model I presume). In my case you can just describe the sound in the text format.Happy to answer any questions!

title: Show HN: CommonForge – Let clients' AI agents work in your codebase safely
author: BUILD3R-Dev
body:
# CommonForge-org/commonforge

Many agents and people changing one project at once, on Cloudflare Workers and Artifacts

- Stars: 0
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 0
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Homepage: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@commonforge-org/cli
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-14T17:33:02Z

## Languages

- CSS
- Dockerfile
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Shell
- TypeScript

## Topics

- agency
- ai-agents
- claude-code
- cloudflare-artifacts
- cloudflare-workers
- coding-agents
- durable-objects
- git
- mcp
- self-hosted

## Top Contributors

- BUILD3R-Dev (6 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 

 Your clients build. Their agents help. You stay in control. 

 
 
 
 
 
 

CommonForge is a self-hosted workspace where an agency, its clients and their coding agents change
a client's website together. Clients ask for changes as tasks. Agents work on each task in an
isolated copy of the code. Every change is checked, previewed on a staging site and approved
before it reaches production, and every accepted version can be restored.

For developers: it runs entirely on **Cloudflare Workers** and **Cloudflare Artifacts**. You
deploy it into your own Cloudflare account with one script, and agents work through a small CLI,
`cforge`.

 
 
 
 ▶ Watch the 8-minute demo on YouTube 
 

| | |
|---|---|
| Getting started checklist on a new project | Tasks board with client tasks, one on staging and one an agent is working on |
| **Getting started** walks a new owner from an empty organization to the first client task live. | **Tasks** (staging mode): client tasks move from Working to In staging, Waiting for approval and Live. |
| Give this task to your agent: one Copy prompt button, the steps by hand folded away | The Change storyboard of a proposal that passed its checks |
| **Give to agent** copies one prompt that a coding agent runs from start to finish: install, sign in, check out, submit. | **The Change storyboard**: what was asked, what changed, what was verified, and the next decision. |
| Versions: the accepted versions, the live one marked | |
| **Versions**: every accepted version, the one production runs, and restore. | |

The screenshots come from the local stack (below), not from fixture data. To regenerate them, run
`pnpm --filter @commonforge-org/web run screenshots`
(apps/web/e2e/readme-screenshots.spec.ts).

## How it works

The path from a new deployment to a client's change in production:

1. **Owner signs in.** Sign-in is by emailed magic link. Only the addresses in the deployment's
 admin list (`COMMONFORGE_ADMIN_EMAILS`) may create an organization.
2. **Organization and project.** One organization per client; a project is one client site. The
 project's Overview shows a **Getting started** checklist that reads its progress from the real
 project state.
3. **Import the code.** *Files → Add* imports a public Git repository as the project's first version.
4. **Release target and first publish.** The project's *Settings → Policy* gets a Release section
 (a ready example is offered), which says how to build the site and which Cloudflare Worker runs
 production. Then *Versions → Publish this version*: prepare, approve publishing, publish.
5. **Staging.** A Staging section in the Policy turns on always-on staging. Staging starts from what
 production runs, so the first publish comes before it.
6. **Invite the client.** *Members → Invite*, role Client, with access to the project. Clients see
 only the projects they are given. Then choose, under *Settings → Access*, what they can do with
 each folder: **Can change** (their agent changes it, and the change goes to staging for review),
 **Read only**, or **No access**. A new client reads only until you choose.
7. **The client asks for a change.** The client creates a task on the **Tasks** board: a title and
 what they want, nothing else. Which folders the agent may change, only read, or never see comes
 from the access the owner set in step 6, not from the client.
8. **An agent does it.** *Give to agent* has one button, **Copy prompt for your agent**. The
 person pastes the prompt into a coding agent that can run commands (the Code tab in Claude
 Desktop, Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, …). The agent installs `cforge` if it is missing, signs in
 with a one-time code that the button puts in the prompt, checks the task out into its own copy
 of the task's folders, does the work and finishes with `cforge submit`. The same steps, to run
 by hand, are folded away under the button.
9. **Staging and review.** The submitted change goes to the shared staging site by itself and moves
 to *In staging*. The client tries it there.
10. **Production.** The client who asked for it (or a developer) promotes it from the board. It
 reaches production once it is approved and published; publishing is a separate, explicit step
 (owners by default).

Without staging, the same work goes through **Changes** instead: *New task*, *Give to agent*,
then *Make proposal* once the agent submits. The proposal opens as a Change storyboard: validation
runs the project's checks, then approve, accept as a new version, and publish are three separate
records. Clients of such a project edit a filtered **edition** copy and send it back as a proposal.

Underneath:

- Every task works in its own isolated Artifacts repository, with short-lived credentials scoped to
 that repository. Clients' editions have no access to the production repository.
- A SQLite Durable Object ledger decides, atomically, what becomes the accepted version. Stale
 proposals are refused, approvals are bound to the exact proposal hash, and restore is a new
 forward version.
- An integration runner in a Cloudflare Sandbox container does the git merge, the checks, the
 preview build and the push. The Artifacts API cannot write, so every write is a `git push` from
 the runner.

The repository also hosts the reusable versioned-workspace engine (`@commonforge-org/*`: core,
ledger, providers, runner protocol, conformance suites) that other products can adopt.

## Architecture

```text
 web app / cforge CLI / agents
            │  HTTPS (session cookie or bearer)
            ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────┐   signed jobs (Queue)   ┌──────────────────────────────┐
 │ commonforge-worker          │ ──────────────────────▶ │ commonforge-runner           │
 │ Hono API, auth, broker      │ ◀────────────────────── │ Sandbox container per job:   │
 │ OrgLedger DO (SQLite)       │   results, credentials  │ git merge/check/push, builds │
 │ D1 directory, outbox, cron  │   (service binding)     └──────────────┬───────────────┘
 └──────┬───────────────┬──────┘                                        │ git push
        │ REST/binding  │                                               ▼
        ▼               ▼                               ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  R2 (assets,      Artifacts: <prefix>-<org>-canonical │ -tasks │ -editions repos      │
  manifests,       └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  exports)         commonforge-preview: token-gated previews from R2 + a container per preview
```

The Worker names are the demo instance's; a bootstrap deployment calls them ` -worker`,
` -runner` and ` -preview`. The HTTP API, deploy prerequisites and known deviations are
in apps/worker/API.md.

Code comments and docs sometimes refer to "plan §…", "PRD §…", "AT-NN" (acceptance tests) or
"Task N". These point to internal planning documents that are not published; the code, the tests
and the docs in this repository are the source of truth.

| Path | Package | What |
|---|---|---|
| `packages/core` | `@commonforge-org/core` | Identities, schemas, hashing, path policy, provider contracts |
| `packages/ledger` | `@commonforge-org/ledger` | Acceptance invariants (pure `planCommit`) over a `LedgerStore` port |
| `packages/provider-cloudflare` | `@commonforge-org/provider-cloudflare` | Artifacts and R2 providers |
| `packages/provider-local-git` | `@commonforge-org/provider-local-git` | Local bare-git provider (tests, offline, exit path) |
| `packages/runner-protocol` | `@commonforge-org/runner-protocol` | Signed runner jobs, materialization plans |
| `packages/conformance` | `@commonforge-org/conformance` | Provider and ledger conformance suites |
| `apps/worker` | `@commonforge-org/worker` | Control-plane Worker + `OrgLedger`/`OpsGate` Durable Objects; also the preview and runner Workers (`src/preview`, `src/sandbox`) |
| `apps/runner` | `@commonforge-org/runner` | Integration runner (Sandbox container image, or a Node process) |
| `apps/web` | `@commonforge-org/web` | Web UI (React + Vite), served by the control-plane Worker |
| `apps/cli` | `@commonforge-org/cli` | Developer CLI, binary `cforge` |
| `apps/demo-agents` | `@commonforge-org/demo-agents` | Orchestrates three real agent sessions working concurrently |
| `fixtures/` | | The demo client project ("Customer Portal") |
| `scripts/` | | Bootstrap, teardown, deploy, the live CI harness, demo helpers |

## Quickstart (local, no credentials)

Requires Node.js 22 or newer, pnpm (the version pinned in `package.json`; `corepack enable`) and git.
Run the whole product on your machine without a Cloudflare account:

```sh
pnpm install
scripts/dev-local.sh          # or: pnpm dev:local; PORT=8813 scripts/dev-local.sh for another port
```

Open and sign in as `owner@agency.e2e.test` (the only address allowed to
create an organization; set `ADMIN_EMAIL=you@example.test` to change it). No email is sent: the
sign-in link is printed in the terminal as
`[commonforge dev] magic link for: ` (and kept in
`apps/worker/.wrangler/dev-local.log`). Open it in the same browser. To use the CLI against it:

```sh
pnpm exec turbo run build --filter=@commonforge-org/cli      # bundles apps/cli/dist/index.js
node apps/cli/dist/index.js login --api-url http://127.0.0.1:8799 --email owner@agency.e2e.test
```

The CLI's sign-in link (`…/auth/cli?code=…`) is printed in the server's terminal too; paste it
when `cforge` asks, or run `cforge login --code `.

This is the stack the local-stack e2e suite runs: the real control-plane Worker under
`wrangler dev -c apps/worker/wrangler.e2e.jsonc`, with local D1, Durable Objects, R2 and queues,
serving the real web app. Cloudflare Artifacts, the integration runner and the Cloudflare API are
in-memory fakes, so git pushes, merges, checks and deploys are simulated, previews do not run, and
everything starts empty on each run. `apps/worker/.dev.vars` is never read.

## Self-host on Cloudflare

`scripts/bootstrap.sh` deploys a complete CommonForge into your own Cloudflare account. It is
idempotent: rerun it to update.

You need Workers Paid, Cloudflare Artifacts and Containers (Sandbox) on the account, Docker on
your machine (the runner and preview images are built locally), Node.js 22+, pnpm and an API token.
The token needs Workers Scripts, Workers R2 Storage, D1, Queues, Workers KV Storage, Containers and
Artifacts: Edit, and Account Settings: Read. The Worker gets its own Artifacts-only token.

```sh
export CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN=… CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID=…   # wrangler + account API (never echoed)
export CF_API_TOKEN=…                                   # the Worker's Artifacts token (Artifacts: Edit)
export COMMONFORGE_DEPLOY_API_TOKEN=…                   # optional: release deploys (Workers Scripts + KV: Edit)

scripts/bootstrap.sh --name acme --email-mode log --admin-emails you@acme.com --smoke   # a test deployment
scripts/bootstrap.sh --name acme --admin-emails you@acme.com,@acme.com \
  --email-from login@acme.com --app-domain forge.acme.com --preview-domain preview.acme.net
scripts/teardown.sh  --name acme                         # list what it created
scripts/teardown.sh  --name acme --yes                   # delete it and verify nothing is left
```

Custom domains and the email sender's domain must be zones on the same Cloudflare account as the
deployment. The app and preview domains must differ: previews run site code and never share the
app's origin. Onboarding the sending domain to Cloudflare Email Service is a manual step that the
script prints.

Prerequisites, every flag, the token scopes, state and ownership rules, and teardown are in
**docs/SELF-HOSTING.md**. It also covers local development against real
Cloudflare resources, and the maintainers' scripts for the project's own demo and CI instances
(`scripts/deploy-live.sh`, `scripts/deploy-ci.sh`, `scripts/ci-live/`).

## Install the CLI

```sh
npm install -g @commonforge-org/cli
```

It needs Node.js 22+ and Git. To run a CLI you changed yourself, build it from the source instead
(Node.js 22+, Git and pnpm):

```sh
git clone https://github.com/CommonForge-org/commonforge.git
cd commonforge
pnpm install
pnpm --filter "@commonforge-org/cli..." build
npm install -g ./apps/cli
```

Then `cforge login --api-url --email `. *Give to agent* in the app shows the
rest, filled in for the task, and its **Copy prompt for your agent** lets the agent do all of this
by itself. (The app's hand-off panel shows the same commands; a self-hosted copy that changes the
CLI without publishing it can set `CLI_PUBLISHED` to `false` in
apps/web/src/lib/handoff.ts to show the source build instead.)

### From Claude or Codex (MCP)

`cforge mcp` gives an AI app tools to sign in, list projects and tasks, create a task, check it
out and submit it. The app's **Account** page shows the setup for each app and makes the one-time
sign-in code:

- **Claude Desktop:** the `commonforge.mcpb` extension from the latest release. Open the file and click Install.
- **Claude Code:** `/plugin install commonforge --marketplace CommonForge-org/commonforge`
- **Codex:** a `[mcp_servers.commonforge]` entry in `~/.codex/config.toml` (see
 apps/cli/README.md).

The plugin and the Codex entry start the server with `npx -y @commonforge-org/cli mcp`, so they
need Node.js 22+ but no separate install.

The tools can do only what the signed-in person can; see docs/LIMITATIONS.md
for what is tested.

## Build and test

```sh
pnpm install
pnpm build          # turbo: every package, the web app, the Worker bundles
pnpm typecheck
pnpm test           # unit and integration tests (miniflare, real git, fakes for Artifacts/runner)

pnpm --filter @commonforge-org/web exec playwright install chromium   # once
pnpm test:e2e        # Playwright: fixture-mode UI + the local stack (no credentials)
pnpm test:fault      # fault injection via COMMONFORGE_CHAOS flags + provider fault conformance
pnpm test:security   # the security acceptance tests across worker, runner, core, runner-protocol, conformance
pnpm test:live       # live-provider tests; need CF_API_TOKEN (CI runs them only when the secret is set)
```

docs/LIMITATIONS.md §8
lists, per suite, what is real and what is faked. CONTRIBUTING.md has the rest.

## Demo

**Watch the demo on YouTube** (8:28, with chapters and captions):
a client's agents and the agency's agents build one feature in parallel, a conflict is caught
before it ships, the change goes through staging to production, and then a fresh deployment is set
up from this repository and a client hands a task to Claude Code.

The project runs its own demo instance of CommonForge on its Cloudflare account. The original
script, beat by beat, is docs/DEMO-SCRIPT.md.

## Spike results

Before anything depended on Artifacts and Sandbox behavior, each assumption the design rests on
was measured on a live Cloudflare account (evidence in `spikes/*/RESULTS.md`).

| | Assumption | Verdict | Consequence |
|---|---|---|---|
| A1 | Stale pushes are refused | PARTIAL: the server accepts `--force`, but never silently last-writer-wins | Every runner push uses `--force-with-lease` against the ledger's sha, one ref per push (`--atomic` is now refused) |
| A2 | Forks are fast and survive parent deletion | PARTIAL: they survive; 2.5 s at 1 MB, ~50 s at 500 MB | Forks and creates run in queue steps. Forks cannot cross namespaces, so task repos are fresh repos seeded by the runner |
| A3 | `git` runs in a Sandbox container and pushes to Artifacts | VERIFIED | Runner = Sandbox container, token injected on egress, internet off |
| A4 | Token revocation stops in-flight pushes | VERIFIED: effective on the next request (~170 ms) | Candidate freeze = token revocation |
| A5 | Custom refs and notes work | PARTIAL: over git yes; REST cannot resolve full ref names | The ledger stores shas; ref listing happens in the runner |
| A6 | `pushed` events arrive within ~5 s | VERIFIED (p95 1.1 s); `repo.forked`/`imported` never arrive | Events are wakeups only, with a periodic sweep as the backstop |
| A7 | Per-candidate preview hostnames | PARTIAL: needs a zone with wildcard DNS | Path-based, token-gated, expiring previews on one dedicated origin |
| A8 | Wrangler ≥ 4.145 with a remote Artifacts binding | VERIFIED | `wrangler dev` always uses real credentials |
| A9 | Rate-limit headroom for 100 task lifecycles | VERIFIED: 0 × 429 over 700 lifecycles | Cap of 25 concurrent fork/token operations per namespace |

## Limitations and what is simulated

**Nothing in the core path is simulated** on a Cloudflare deployment (yours, or the demo
instance): real Artifacts repositories, real `git push` from a real Sandbox container, the real
Durable Object ledger, R2, Queues, Email Service and real `wrangler deploy` releases. The local
quickstart is the exception: it fakes Artifacts, the runner and the Cloudflare API, and says so.

Also labelled as not live:

- The web app's **fixture mode** (`VITE_COMMONFORGE_FIXTURE=1`) runs the UI on in-memory sample
 data, always under a "Fixture mode" banner. Only the fixture-mode e2e suite uses it.
- The e2e, fault and security suites replace Artifacts, the runner and the Cloudflare API with test
 doubles, and they say so.

The main shortcuts of this build:

- Previews share one origin, the preview Worker's (a path per preview, token-gated, expiring).
- There is one ledger Durable Object per organization.
- Stale bases are refused, with no automatic rebase.
- Sign-in is by magic link only.
- No ArtifactFS: export is plain git bundles plus asset manifests.
- No private Git import. A confirmed ZIP intake creates its resources empty: copying the archive in
 needs a runner step that does not exist yet.

The full, honest list is in docs/LIMITATIONS.md.

## Contributing, security, licence

Contributing: CONTRIBUTING.md and the code of conduct.
Reporting a vulnerability: SECURITY.md (not a public issue).

The code is MIT © 2026 CommonForge contributors. Third-party licences:
THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md.

The CommonForge name and the logos in `brand/` are trademarks and are not covered by the MIT
licence; see brand/README.md.

title: Show HN: Transform your GitHub activity graph into a work of art
author: evgy
body:
# freaker2k7/github-activity-graph-populator

- Stars: 9
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 9
- Open issues: 0
- License: Apache License 2.0
- Default branch: master
- Created: 2026-10-14T21:38:28Z

## Languages

- HTML
- Python

## Top Contributors

- freaker2k7 (23 contributions)

---

## README

# GitHub Activity Graph Populator

GitHub Build

GAGP (GitHub Activity Graph Populator) is a tool to populate your GitHub activity graph the way you like — or make it look super busy!

**Zero** dependencies, **99.53%** test coverage and **PyPI MFA** enabled making it more secure and lightweight 🚀

## Available Patterns

- Tree
- Checkmark
- Wave
- Smile
- Flower
- **Custom** (see details below)

Or make it look super busy using the busy mode.

## Demo

You can see a live demo on my own GitHub profile here.

Before 
 2012: Before it looked like this... 

After 
 2012: Now, it looked like this! This is the flower pattern. 

Before 
 2013: Before it was like this... 

After 
 2013: Now, it's like this! This is the tree pattern and yeah, my design skills definitely need improvement but it's really hard to draw on a 7 pixel grid 😅 

*Note: I have a huge number of contributions on my GitHub profile, the images are from the years 2012 and 2013, back then my activity on GitHub was much lower.*

*Another Note: On the way, I discovered I can write history before I was a user which opened the 2012 tab and I cound see the year.*

## TL;DR

Originally, I wanted to represent my Bitbucket activity (where I have over 250 private repositories vs ~50 public ones on GitHub plus a few dozens private ones that apparenly isn't shown on the activity graph for the public) onto my GitHub activity graph, but I didn't want to mess with syncying jobs and dealing with API's when it's just git...
So I decided to just draw a nice pattern on my GitHub activity graph instead, using a nifty git hack I learned over the years; either way, the volume of my commits across GH, BB, AWS and a few other platforms is so high that it doesn't really matter 😜

But I thought it would be fun to create a tool that allows anyone to visually populate their GitHub activity graph with custom patterns 😇

## Installation

```bash
pip install github-activity-graph-populator
```

## Usage

**First** create a public repository on GitHub.

**Then**, after you install the package, you can use the command line.
See the help message for available commands:

```text
$ gagp --help

usage: main.py [-h] [--repo REPO] [--force-push] [--filename FILENAME] [--folder FOLDER] [--from-date FROM_DATE] [--to-date TO_DATE] [--mode {matrix,busy}] [--matrix {tree,checkmark,wave,smile,flower,custom}]
               [--custom-matrix CUSTOM_MATRIX] [--max-intensity MAX_INTENSITY] [--cleanup] [--test]

Populate GitHub activity graph

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  --repo REPO           Name of the repository to populate in the format of <github_username>/<repository_name> (default: None)
  --force-push          Force push to the remote repository (default: False)
  --filename FILENAME   Name of the file to create and commit (default: README.md)
  --folder FOLDER       Folder to create temporary files in (default: None)
  --from-date FROM_DATE
                        Start date for populating GitHub activity graph (default: None)
  --to-date TO_DATE     End date for populating GitHub activity graph (default: None)
  --mode {matrix,busy}  Mode for populating GitHub activity graph (default: matrix)
  --matrix {tree,checkmark,wave,smile,flower,custom}
                        Matrix style for populating GitHub activity graph (default: tree)
  --custom-matrix CUSTOM_MATRIX
                        Path to custom tile style for populating GitHub activity graph. There must be 7 rows and at least 1 column in the matrix and it should be a plain text file. The values in the matrix represent the color 0-4 from
                        white to dark green (default: None)
  --max-intensity MAX_INTENSITY
                        Average number of commits per day [only used for 'busy' mode] (default: 10)
  --cleanup             Run cleanup after populating GitHub activity graph (default: False)
  --test                Run in test mode (default: False)
```

*Note: The date format for the `--from-date` and `--to-date` options is `YYYY-MM-DD`.*

*Another Note: As GitHub was released in 2008, the minimum `from-date` is 2008-01-01.*

### Examples

```bash
# Colorful tree pattern
gagp --matrix tree --from 2013-01-01 --to 2013-04-01 --repo your-github-username/your-repo-name

# Or make it look super busy
gagp --mode busy --from 2013-01-01 --to 2013-04-01 --repo your-github-username/your-repo-name
```

You can create your own custom matrix by using the `--matrix custom` and `--custom-matrix` options.

```bash
gagp --matrix custom --custom-matrix path/to/your/custom_matrix.txt --from 2013-01-01 --to 2013-04-01 --repo your-github-username/your-repo-name
```

when your `custom_matrix.txt` looks something like this:

```
0123411
1111111
1111111
1111111
1112211
1133311
1111111
```

There must be 7 rows and at least 1 column in the matrix and it should be a plain text file.
The values in the matrix represent the color 0-4 from white to dark green.

You can generate your own custom matrix using any tile builder (see the contribution guide for more information).

(Optionally) You can force push the changes if the repository is not clean:

```bash
gagp --mode busy --from 2013-01-01 --to 2013-04-01 --repo your-github-username/your-repo-name --force-push
```

*NOTE: Though I don't recommend it as the re-caching of the GitHub activity graph can take some time. I suggest using a new repo or deleting and recreating the existing one as this is kind of a "dummy" repository that we just need to update its history.*

#### Output

When running the cli command, you will see output similar to the following:

```bash
$ gagp --from-date 2012-01-01 --to-date 2012-12-30 --matrix flower --repo freaker2k7/2012-flowers

[INFO] 2026-10-15 14:07:18,795: github-activity-graph-populator >> Temporary input folder created at: /tmp/gagp-s4y5ok57
```

title: Show HN: Axiom, a general-purpose model for causal discovery
author: maxpagels
body:
Max Pagels 
 Axiom
 A general-purpose model for causal discovery. Give it a table of data, and it drafts a causal graph of what is likely to cause what.
 🤗 maxpagels/axiom-base 
 Model on Hugging Face Model card Weights 
 3.8M parameters · fp32 safetensors · 15 MB
Contents
 Introduction 
 Causal graphs, briefly 
 Why discovery is hard 
 What to do with the output 
 Running Axiom 
 Using intervention data 
 Limitations 
 Benchmarks 
Introduction
 Drafting a causal graph, a representation of what is thought to cause what, is often the first step in causal inference. This process is known as causal discovery .
 Discovery is usually done manually, through a blend of stakeholder interviews and domain expertise. Ideally, the result is a correct directed graph of the causal process of interest. In practice it will never be perfect, but even an imperfect graph is valuable. A partially correct graph still encodes a great deal of knowledge: which variables are plausibly related, which are almost certainly not, and the direction of influence for at least some relationships.
 Automated causal discovery aims to speed up this traditionally manual process by inferring such partial graphs directly from data. Axiom is an open general-purpose model built for this task.
Causal graphs, briefly
 A causal graph is a set of variables connected by arrows. An arrow from one variable to another means the first is a direct cause of the second: change it, and the second changes too, all else being equal. The absence of an arrow is just as informative, since it claims there is no direct influence.
Fig. 1 — A small causal graph. Arrows point from cause to effect. In the example above, every variable is a continuous measurement: temperature in degrees, irrigation in litres, evaporation and soil moisture in millimetres, crop yield in kilograms per hectare. Higher temperatures lead farmers to irrigate more and also increase evaporation. Irrigation adds water to the soil while evaporation removes it, and soil moisture in turn drives crop yield. Note what the graph does not say: irrigation has no direct effect on yield. Its influence flows entirely through soil moisture.
 Irrigation and evaporation will also be correlated in data, even though neither causes the other. Both share a common cause, temperature. Telling apart relationships like these is precisely what causal discovery tries to do.
Why discovery is hard
 Inferring causal direction from observational data alone can be impossible in principle. The same data can arise from entirely different causal structures. Take two variables, A and B. A world where A causes B and a world where B causes A can produce exactly the same joint distribution. With linear relationships and Gaussian noise, for instance, the two are indistinguishable no matter how many rows you collect.
 World 1 A → B 
 A ~ N ( 0 , 1 )
 B = 0.8 A + ε 
 ε ~ N ( 0 , 0.36 )
World 2 B → A 
 B ~ N ( 0 , 1 )
 A = 0.8 B + ε 
 ε ~ N ( 0 , 0.36 )
In both worlds A and B have mean 0, variance 1 and correlation 0.8, so they produce the same bivariate normal distribution. No amount of observational data can tell them apart. The basic idea behind Axiom is that, despite this, one can do much better than random guessing. Axiom is a general-purpose model with attention across both rows and columns, letting it reason jointly about individual samples and the relationships between variables. It is trained on synthetic data drawn from a wide range of causal mechanisms. Real-world processes are rarely the perfectly symmetric worst case, and they leave subtle asymmetries in their data.
What to do with the output
 The graph Axiom returns is not meant to be perfect. Think of it as a first draft: a starting point that is refined with domain knowledge. Go through it with the people who know the process best. Remove edges that are physically or logically impossible, add relationships you know exist, flip arrows that point the wrong way, and flag the ones nobody is sure about.
 Once the graph is good enough, there are several things you can do with it:
 Estimate causal effects
 The graph tells you which variables to adjust for, and which to leave alone, when estimating the effect of one variable on another. That way you avoid both confounding and bias from conditioning on the wrong variables (hint: I made Formative for this purpose).
Test your assumptions
 Every graph implies conditional independencies that can be checked against data. If the data contradicts one, part of the graph is likely wrong.
Prioritise experiments
 Edges that are uncertain or that matter a lot for a decision are natural candidates for targeted interventions. Their results can then be fed back into Axiom as intervention data.
Simulate what-if scenarios
 Fit a structural model on top of the graph to predict what happens when you change a variable, rather than merely observe it.
Running Axiom
 Install the package straight from the Hugging Face repository:
 bash pip install "git+https://huggingface.co/maxpagels/axiom-base" 
 Then load the model and pass it a table. Axiom reads the whole dataset in a single forward pass. Missing values can be left as NaN .
 python from axiom import Axiom , discover 
model = Axiom . from_pretrained ( "maxpagels/axiom-base" ) 
 g = discover (model, df) # pandas DataFrame or (n, d) array; NaN = missing 
g . edges # [(cause, effect, probability), ...] 
 g . edge_probs () # (d, d) matrix of P(i -> j) 
 g . confounded # (d, d) 0/1 matrix: likely hidden common cause, no edge 
 discover standardises each column the same way as during training, so pass your data as-is. Only use axiom.preprocess if you want to call the model directly.
 What comes back
 For every pair of variables, Axiom predicts probabilities over five classes, which are then decoded into an acyclic graph:
 none No direct causal edge. 
 i → j / j → i A direct edge, with direction. 
 undirected Linked, but the direction is not identifiable from the data. 
 confounded No direct edge, but a hidden common cause. 
Recommended use
 Rows 256 or more works best; usable from around 100, below which results get unreliable. Tables over 512 rows are split into random 512-row subsets whose predictions are averaged (8 by default, raise n_subsets to use more of a large table). 
 Variables Trained on 3 to 25. On simulated data it held up to 100 with no loss in accuracy; beyond 25 on real data is untested. Memory grows quickly with the variable count: roughly 1 GB on CPU at 100 variables, 3 GB at 200. 
 Interventions If any rows come from experiments, label all of them. Unlabelled experimental rows act like hidden causes and can produce wrong or reversed edges. 
 Output Treat edges, and especially directions, as ranked hypotheses to check rather than a verdict. 
Using intervention data
 If some rows come from experiments, where a variable was deliberately set rather than observed, tell Axiom which ones. Interventions break symmetry and can sharply improve direction accuracy.
 python # One entry per row: None = observational, otherwise the 
 # column(s) that row's experiment targeted. An (n, d) bool mask also works. 
 targets = [ None , "PKC" , [ "PKA" , "PIP3" ] , None , ...] 
g = discover (model, df, interventions = targets) 
 Label every experimental row. Rows that came from an experiment but are left unlabelled look like the work of a hidden cause, and can produce wrong or reversed edges.
Limitations
 Axiom is trained only on synthetic data. Real data that differs from that prior, such as cycles, time series, selection bias or truly discrete mechanisms, is out of distribution.
 Hidden-confounder detection is weak. Treat the confounded output as a hint.
 Directions on real data can come out reversed. The synthetic training data lets the model infer direction from which variable is more predictable from the others, and real systems often show the opposite pattern. A fix to the training data is planned.
 Causal discovery from observational data rests on assumptions. Validate important edges with domain knowledge or experiments.
Benchmarks
 Benchmark results are available on the Hugging Face model page .

comments.text: Hey great question! WebContext owns an output buffer (i.e., RenderBuffer) that components write HTML into directly, avoiding intermediate allocations and copying. It needs to be mutable for this reason. This is one of the key ways we're able to make Proa the fastest server-side rendering engine on the market.By default, WebContext composes RenderBuffer (but it can be overriden via generics) which uses fixed-size 4 KiB pages. When a page runs out of room, it adds another page without moving the HTML already written. This avoids copying the accumulated output during growth! Its designed to be a performance improvement over Vec<u8>For context, the problem with Vec<u8> is that every time a vector reaches maximum capacity, it has to reallocate a new area of memory (typically 2x larger than the previous allocation) and then copy everything into that new buffer. This adds a ton of overhead, especially if you're writing large pages.Checkout https://github.com/Proa-Labs/proa/blob/384136f87fc9f91747477... if you're curious about RenderBuffer's design

comments.author: burnrate
comments.text:
> This might be a silly question, but why 2 views for html and markdown?No such thing as silly questions! Yes there are cases where it can be inferred from one to the other, but in many cases you may want to be very specific about how you author the markdown view. I'll give you a few examples:1. Custom components: For example, let's say you have a carousel component. It's not really straightforward to infer the markdown from this. But you probably want the carousel to render as a series of markdown image tags. A custom view would be helpful for this. Same goes for Calendars, SVG charts, Diagrams, form inputs, tabs, popovers, and more.2. Information omission: Agents don't need all of the information on your page. For example, a dark/light button... probably doesn't need a markdown equivalent. But a button that is an anchor tag that links to another page, probably you should keep. So having the ability to custom author the markdown render target based on the data it's rendering is helpful.One of the unique aspects of Proa's authoring model is that it supports composability of Markdown components, just like JSX, which is I think one of its standout features.
